title: Homeward bound
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
FIVE months after Somali pirates captured an oil tanker carrying a 19-member multinational crew, Somali maritime police have recovered the vessel off the coast of Puntland. The Foreign Office has confirmed five casualties — out of the 10 Pakistani seamen, three have died with four wounded during the rescue operation; a total of five sailors lost their lives. Despite efforts — social media videos show hostages asking the Pakistani government to engage with their captors; hapless families staging protests and facing police brutality, and even calling on foreign governments and international agencies to take coordinated action — losses could not be averted. Regrettably, a forceful approach involving collaborative action with Indonesia, India and Sri Lanka was missing on the part of the government. Hence, this homeward journey is bittersweet.
Seajacks by pirate gangs had subsided around the Gulf of Aden and the Indian Ocean. But, fuelled by political upheaval, poverty and aid cuts, piracy is back with a vengeance. Recent instances suggest that, due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, this route needs amplified transnational patrolling. Clearly, this year’s tally of over 100 ships struck and 40 hijacked with 15 attacks in April alone confirms that a prime trade passage has become perilous. We cannot lose more time. An international naval cover, comprising satellite information, emergency services, and a tracking dashboard effective in strife-torn waterways for navigational safety, is vital. In short, only a modern maritime protection framework alongside contingency plans can prevent future shocks. Meanwhile, local labour rights bodies must protect sailors from the coercive policies of shipping companies and other patrons. Global trade relies on mariners. They must have the power to choose secure routes without fear of repercussions. Additionally, the government is obligated to provide compensation to affected families and to ensure that no distressed citizen faces official apathy.
Published in Dawn, October 1st, 2026

title: Fixing bond markets
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE plan to deepen the domestic local currency bond market by allowing the public to trade government securities through the stock market should help address a weakness long concealed by the sovereign’s easy access to bank borrowings. Pakistan’s large government securities market lacks the depth and diversification needed to allow securities to be widely held, actively traded and efficiently priced. Banks, holding about 78pc of government securities with sovereign paper accounting for roughly 62pc of their assets, have therefore little reason to seek ‘riskier’ private borrowers. Consequently, small firms, farmers and potential homebuyers struggle to obtain credit. The proposed reforms recognise this structural weakness. More predictable and market-based issuance, greater secondary-market liquidity, a functioning repo market and a broader investor base are all necessary. Allowing individuals to trade exchange-listed government securities through their banks should also improve access and price discovery. But can the reforms change how the market works?
That requires breaking the banks’ dominance. Pension funds, insurance companies, mutual funds, retail investors, and eventually, foreign investors must become bigger participants. They need both access and incentives to hold and trade rupee securities. Secondary-market liquidity is equally important. Primary dealers should have incentives to make markets rather than merely participate in government auctions. The proposed review of the primary-dealer framework and securities-lending facility could help. The IMF should push this logic further. The government must borrow less from commercial banks. Reducing bank borrowing would force greater reliance on actual market financing, creating room for banks to lend to productive private activity.
The market should also be broadened beyond government debt. The government could require SOEs to raise at least one-third of all future local currency borrowing through bonds. This would create more issuers, diversify instruments and maturities, and expose SOE borrowing to greater market scrutiny. Demand can be boosted through targeted tax incentives for investors holding local currency bonds issued by SOEs and private companies. Such incentives should encourage longer-term investment. Further, transparently priced government securities across maturities can provide benchmarks against which private companies price their own debt. Over time, this could reduce the economy’s overreliance on bank lending. That said, the government must avoid treating the bond market reform as a way to finance itself more easily. A deeper market should reduce refinancing risks, improve monetary policy transmission and redirect savings to productive investment. The measure of success cannot be the number of bonds issued. It must be who buys them, how actively they trade, how liquid the market becomes and whether businesses have better access to long-term capital.

title: Misunderstanding Pakistan
author: none@none.com (Basil Nabi Malik)
content:
THE foundational basis of Pakistan and the objectives behind the country’s creation remain a subject of debate. One side emphasises religion above all else and argues that the basis for creating Pakistan was Islam itself. On the other hand, some commentators contend that Pakistan was created for the residents of specific regions, the majority of whom were Muslims, so that they could live their lives freely and without subjugation. Although religion was undeniably important, the primary goal was to secure the people’s free will and freedom.
Even without debating which worldview is accurate — if any — we can agree on a few truths. First, Pakistan was born through the will and struggle of its people. Second, the decision to create Pakistan was achieved and affirmed through their votes. And finally, Pakistan was brought into being through a process that can, arguably, be considered democratic.
In essence, the establishment of Pakistan was people-centric. And when the ‘people’ in question share a single culture, language, history, and geography, it becomes easy to categorise them as a monolithic community with a singular identity. However, when a nation comprises diverse ethnic groups with distinct cultures and histories running parallel to one another, neatly situated in separate regions of a land seeking to unite, the mechanics of political representation necessarily change.
Unlike a single monolithic community represented by a unitary voice, multiple distinct communities seeking union often have separate representatives, at least initially, to protect their specific interests within the broader polity. The union is not the merging of a single people, but a voluntary arrangement among distinct communities with shared goals. To achieve this, these communities, through their representatives, discuss, negotiate, and agree on the union’s dynamics, defining which powers are transferred to the central state and which remain local.
Commentators frequently overlook the foundational premise of the nation itself.
This process transfers sovereignty from individual communities to a united entity that becomes greater than the sum of its parts, while protecting regional rights and identities. The goal of such a union is a better shared future; unity is seen as offering greater benefits than division. This fusion of distinct groups into a singular national framework is the essence of entering into a social contract.
Pakistan, which is home to diverse ethnicities and communities, is said to have entered into precisely this type of union right after independence. For many, that social contract was earlier epitomised by the Lahore Resolution of 1940; for others, it was crystallised in the 1973 Constitution. Whichever document one examines, the formal recognition and celebration of diversity are recurring themes.
Pakistan was always intended to be pluralistic, with communities coming together to pool their resources and cede certain freedoms for the collective good. Pakistan came into being for them, not despite them. Abdul Wali Khan articulated well the vision of what Pakistan could be, noting that despite their distinct identities, the federating units were akin to “flowers with their distinct colours and fragrance” that “blend into a bouquet, manifesting their unity in diversity”. Ultimately, the country’s founding idea is rooted in protecting its people, their cultures, languages, and rights. That is what it ought to be, and whether anyone likes it or not, this is what it was always meant to be.
Why is this discussion so critical today? Because when commentators debate whether creating more provinces is necessary for a prosperous Pakistan, whether local governments need to be strengthened, or whether addressing the missing persons issue is key to winning hearts and minds, they frequently overlook the foundational premise of the nation itself. This premise is intrinsically linked to the people’s will and aspirations. As with any major decision, altering provincial boundaries, whether by creating fewer or more provinces or restructuring existing ones, must remain a choice driven directly by the people whose goals are bound to Pakistan’s genesis. Similarly, the people must decide the role of local governments, and the resolution of the missing persons crisis must be as great a priority as the people make it.
If you remove the popular will from this decision-making process, you strike at the core of Pakistan’s founding identity. You not only carve up administrative boundaries and dismiss popularly held convictions, but also dismember the very vision articulated in the 1940 Resolution, codified in the 1973 Constitution, and reaffirmed through the 18th Amendment.
Democracy is neither a luxury that Pakistan cannot afford nor is it a failed concept. If anything, when allowed to function, democratic governance is the single thread that has kept this federation together throughout its turbulent history. It maintains the vital link between the state and the populace that gave it birth. If new administrative units are to be carved out or other consequential decisions to be taken, those decisions belong exclusively to the public, not to self-appointed arbiters who claim to know better than the citizens themselves.
After all, armies did not create Pakistan; the people’s vote did. War tacticians did not envision Pakistan; politicians, lawyers, and civilians did. A war did not lead the nation to independence; a barrister did. Consequently, the bond between the Pakistani state and its citizens is as intrinsic and consequential as water is to fish, instruments are to musicians, and ‘national interest’ is to our armed forces.
If you remove the people from decision-making, you strip away the soul of the country. What remains is merely a land without a people, a people without a voice, and a country without a purpose, with nothing left but despair.
The writer is a lawyer based in Karachi.

title: The privatisation of resilience
author: syed.siddiq.hussain
content:
What happens when powerful people stop believing that the future can be salvaged, and they instead start preparing to survive its destruction?

That is the unsettling question at the heart of End Times Fascism: And the Fight for the Living World, the new book by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. The book argues that a new political formation is emerging from the convergence of religious fundamentalists, ethno-nationalists, Silicon Valley billionaires and other reactionaries. What connects them is not necessarily a common political programme, but an increasingly apocalyptic imagination: the conviction that some catastrophic rupture is coming and that they will somehow be the ones to survive it.

Klein calls this "end-times fascism". Unlike twentieth-century fascism, which sought national rebirth through authoritarianism and exclusion, today's far right increasingly wants to prepare for a world shaped by climate change, resource scarcity, mass migration and other crises.

Klein's ongoing work for more than the last two decades has explored the growing power of corporations, how elites exploit crises for their own benefit, and now how the wealthy seek to insulate themselves from catastrophe.

In a recent interview about the book, she offers a jolting observation about wealth itself: "Wealth has its own deranging effects." Humans, she observes, need stories to make sense of the world around them. The ultra-rich are no different: they, too, need stories to explain why they possess so much while others have so little. The answer can become a story of superiority: that there is something about the wealthy person that justifies their extraordinary share of resources, with the implicit conclusion that inequality is deserved.

This is where Klein's argument becomes particularly relevant to the Global South.

In wealthy countries, apocalyptic politics may take the form of the eccentric fantasy of billionaires to build bunkers or imagine escaping to Mars. In countries such as Pakistan, however, catastrophe is already part of everyday political and economic life. Floods, heatwaves, water insecurity and toxic air are no longer distant possibilities. Yet, the consequences of these emergent threats are not distributed equally. Those who can afford it can protect themselves from the harshest forms of the climate apocalypse.

People with money can purchase safer land, gated housing, private security, generators, solar power, air conditioning, private healthcare and reliable water supplies. They can move away from areas threatened by flooding or extreme heat. They can send their children abroad and, if they have the means, can even build new lives elsewhere.

For poorer citizens, resilience often means trying to navigate weak and apathetic public systems. They remain dependent on increasingly resource constrained public hospitals, schools, water supplies and infrastructure.

Even something as mundane as an air purifier has become a marker of class. In Lahore, where toxic air is a recurring crisis, the air purifier has acquired something of the status once occupied by the UPS during the worst of load-shedding: a private technological solution to a public failure.

The idea of "end-times fascism" can thus be extended beyond the politics of the American far right. In the Global South, it can take the form of a politics of elite insulation: the acceptance that public systems will fail, accompanied by the assumption that those with wealth will somehow be protected.

In Pakistan, where the impacts of the global climate crisis are being acutely felt and the country has limited capacity to contend with these threats, the question becomes: who gets to adapt? If resilience must be purchased, it becomes a privilege.

Climate change is not only making Pakistan more unequal; it is also illustrating how affluence determines who can secure some protection from its effects, making those who can afford it increasingly indifferent to the need to address these public problems.

That is not disaster mitigation. It is the privatisation of resilience.

title: Three revolutions
author: none@none.com (F.S. Aijazuddin)
content:
THE past 250 years have seen a tsunami of revolutions — the American, the French, the Chinese, and imitating them, the Cuban. Their waves swept across the world, impacting us today and, as Chairman Mao Zedong predicted, they will affect tomorrow’s history. This year, friends of America celebrate its first 250 years; its detractors see them as its last 250 years. America enjoys the pre-eminence that capitalism promised — at a Faustian price, redeemable in US dollars. America is discomfited by Russia, a perpetual migraine; China, a recurring malaise; and Cuba, an irritating thorn in its side.
A recent book by Simon Hall — Three Revolutions: Russia, China and Cuba (2025) — examines the genesis of their social upheavals. Interestingly, he links them to three writers (all American) who happened to be in the right place at the right time: John Reed, who in 1917 witnessed the ignition of the Russian Revolution; Edgar Snow, who met Mao and those who had survived the gruelling Long March of 1934-35; and Herbert Matthews, a New York Times correspondent, who in 1957 wriggled into Cuba and watched Fidel Castro’s underfunded but determined bid to depose Gen Batista. The three wrote accounts of their experiences and interaction with leaders, especially Lenin, Mao and Fidel Castro. They provided authentic, corrective insights into the social cataclysms that continue to be misunderstood by the West.
In 1917, Reed sees the storming of the czar’s Winter Palace in Petrograd (now St Petersburg). Looters are prevented from despoiling the palace’s treasures and opulent furnishings by “self-appointed sentinels”, who shout: “Comrades! Don’t take anything! This is the property of the people!” Another diligent sailor guarding the Winter Palace refuses entry to a new provisional government minister and the city’s mayor. “What will you do?” the two unarmed civilians ask him. The burly sailor replies: “We will spank you, and if necessary, shoot you!”
On meeting Lenin, Reed notices that he “looks through you with those terrible eyes … of being intensely interested”. Reed’s book Ten Days That Shook the World (1919) quotes Trotsky’s recollection of how Lenin, on Oct 10, 1917, scribbled a call for armed insurrection “hastily … with the gnawed end of a pencil on a sheet of paper from a child’s notebook ruled in squares”.
Internecine conflicts have replaced revolutions.
Lenin’s “sealed train” journey, from Switzerland across Germany and Finland to Russia, was more comfortable than the privations of the Long March. Of the 100,000 troops and party stalwarts who started from Jiangxi, only 6,000 or so reached Yan’an, 9,000 kilometres away. Edgar Snow first met Mao in 1936. He described him as a “gaunt, rather Lincolnesque figure … with a face of intellectual shrewdness”. He attributes Mao’s genius to “his uncanny ability to embody the demands of millions of his fellow citizens — above all, the peasantry”.
Snow converted memories of a three-month stay in China into a book — Red Star over China (1937). It had an immeasurable impact, even in Washington’s highest circles. President Franklin D. Roosevelt’s secretary of the interior, H. Ickes, remarked presciently that “any people that can do what the Red Army did during the Long March and after” were “positively invincible”.
Simon Hall’s inclusion of the Cuban revolution of 1956-59 may appear surprising until one reads how Castro achieved it. Arrested by Gen Batista’s soldiers, Castro’s life is spared by a compassionate lieutenant who tells his troops: “Don’t shoot. You can’t kill ideas”. Castro is tried and sentenced to 15 years in jail. In court, he makes a defiant spe­ech: “I do not fear prison[.] Condemn me. It does not matter. History will absolve me.”
Batista made the mistake of granting Castro an early am­­nesty. Castro repaid the favour by returning to Cuba from exile in Mexico. In 1956, he landed in Granma — “a creaking, leaking leisure yacht”. It was less “a landing than a shipwreck”. Harassed by Batista’s soldiers, Castro hid in the Sierra Maestra mountains — the commander of “two men, a couple of rifles and 120 rounds of ammunition”. There, he is joined by his brother Raúl, who brought five guns. Castro says, with bravado: “That makes seven. We have won the war!”
Herbert Matthews interviewed Castro in his Sierra hideout, writing afterwards: “He has caught the imagination of the youth of Cuba [because] he is an educated, dedicated fanatic, a man of ideals, of courage, and of remarkable qualities of leadership.” Within three years, Castro toppled the US-supported Gen Batista.
In the 21st century, internecine conflicts have replaced revolutions. Autocracies may blindfold eyes that dare to see. Revolutions, though, like tsunamis, are unpredictable. They do not wait for submissive activists who, in Lenin’s words, sit in “armchair ideas” plotting “armchair action”.
The writer is an author.

The article details key moments and leaders of these revolutions: Lenin's leadership in the Russian Revolution, Mao's genius and the arduous Long March in China, and Fidel Castro's defiant struggle and eventual victory in Cuba.

It concludes by contrasting historical revolutions with 21st-century internecine conflicts but emphasizes the unpredictable and transformative power of genuine uprisings, which do not wait for 'armchair action'.

title: Water shortage
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THAT the country is entering the Rabi season with an anticipated water shortage of nearly 25pc, the lowest carryover since 2021, is a matter of serious concern. It is likely to hit the next wheat harvest hard — a staple food crop already under stress owing to bad policies. Wheat output fell to 27.5 million tonnes against a 29.7m target and 32m consumption last season, requiring imports. Now farmers face less water. The shortage is not simply a consequence of poor rainfall or hydrology. Water management decisions have also contributed to it. According to a report in this paper, more than 1MAF of water that could have been conserved was released from reservoirs during Kharif. Political pressure reportedly played a role in these releases. If so, the episode exposes an entrenched weakness in national water management. The fact that the country continues to manage water driven by short-term political needs instead of long-term planning must change.
The management of reservoirs should follow transparent rules based on water availability, crop requirements, environmental needs and future risks. There is also a need to distinguish between wasteful releases and legitimate environmental flows. Rivers cannot be reduced to irrigation channels. They require water to sustain their ecosystems. Environmental needs must be properly calculated and incorporated into planning. The coming shortage will also revive the old provincial dispute. Irsa will have to distribute a smaller pool of water among the provinces. The existing arrangements already generate disagreement, particularly over how shortages should be shared. Severe shortages will intensify interprovincial tensions — which the centre must prevent. Decisions should be based on verifiable data, in accordance with the Water Apportionment Accord, 1991. The government must also invest in irrigation efficiency and water conservation. Farmers cannot be expected to bear the cost of decades of institutional neglect. The larger failure is that our policymakers still treat water shortages as emergencies rather than as a permanent national constraint. That approach is not sustainable. Climate change makes water availability less predictable while population and food demand continue to rise. The country, therefore, needs a water policy that looks beyond one crop, one harvest and one province. It needs to conserve more, waste less and plan years ahead.
Published in Dawn, September 30th, 2026

title: Kashmir unresolved
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
SEVEN years after India revoked occupied Kashmir’s limited autonomy, disquiet continues in the disputed region over the prevailing state of affairs. Even loyalist parties in India’s good books are not happy. This was reflected in a resolution passed by the held region’s assembly on Monday, which called for a restoration of statehood that was scrapped when the Indian constitution’s Article 370 was abrogated in 2019. The occupied area’s chief minister, Omar Abdullah, claimed that statehood was “our right”. BJP lawmakers termed the resolution “anti-national”. Two similar resolutions have been passed over the years by the IHK legislature.
The problem goes far deeper than the restoration of the status quo ante that existed before August 2019. The core issue is the Kashmiris’ right to self-determination, which India has been blocking since the division of the subcontinent. Unless this core issue is addressed with justice, the problem will linger as Kashmiris in the occupied territory are denied their fundamental rights. While speaking at the UN General Assembly, Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif also highlighted the Kashmir issue, saying that Kashmiris had been waiting “for eight decades” for the UN to fulfil its commitments. He also pointed out the human rights violations that India has carried out against the Kashmiri population. Turkiye’s President Recep Erdogan, while speaking at the UNGA, similarly called for a resolution of the Kashmir question as per the “relevant resolutions”.
The human rights situation in the disputed region is very grim. A UN report from November 2025 has condemned the arbitrary arrests, suspicious deaths in custody, torture and “discriminatory treatment of Kashmiri and Muslim communities”. Held Kashmir’s wounds cannot be left to fester. The people of Kashmir, including even those politicians who were or are close to New Delhi, are chafing under the post-Article 370 regime in the held region. Along with rights abuses, there is also alarm over the demographic changes in IHK, as the Kashmiris are being turned into a minority in their own land. The just solution lies in India addressing the issue through a trilateral dialogue involving the legitimate representatives of the Kashmiri people and Pakistan. India’s rulers can continue to believe the fiction that occupied Kashmir is an ‘integral’ part of their country. But that does nothing to address the dissatisfaction that both the common Kashmiri and the political elite of the region feel towards Indian rule. The dispute has poisoned all chances of normalisation in South Asia. Instead of arrogantly dismissing talk of freedom, India’s rulers need to listen to voices from IHK, and together with Pakistan, work towards a just solution to this dispute.

title: The geography we cannot change
author: Durdana Najam
content:
Long after today's governments have gone, Pakistan and Afghanistan will still share the same mountains, passes, tribes, markets and frontier. That simple geographical truth should matter more than the anger of the present moment.

Relations between Islamabad and Kabul have rarely appeared as dangerous as they do today. Pakistan accuses the Afghan Taliban authorities of allowing the TTP and other militants to use Afghan territory for attacks inside Pakistan. Kabul rejects the allegation and accuses Pakistan of violating Afghan sovereignty. Air strikes, border clashes and competing accusations have gradually turned a security dispute into something close to direct confrontation between two states that have neither the geographical space nor the economic luxury for permanent hostility.

The difficulties are old. Afghanistan opposed Pakistan's entry into the United Nations in 1947 and has contested the Durand Line ever since. The Soviet invasion, the arrival of millions of refugees in Pakistan and the years of the Afghan jihad tied the two societies together. After 2001, each side blamed the other for the instability that followed. When the Taliban returned to power in 2021, many in Pakistan expected a more manageable western border. Instead, the TTP became the central dispute.

The record since then shows a gradual shift. Pakistan's early strikes in Afghanistan in 2022 and 2024 were limited and followed by quick de-escalation. In 2025 Islamabad also pursued diplomacy: visits to Kabul, a trilateral meeting with China in Beijing, an agreement to raise diplomatic ties to ambassador level, and a framework for a joint feasibility study of the Uzbekistan-Afghanistan-Pakistan railway. When attacks continued regardless, the approach hardened.

The Taliban's failure to rein in the TTP cannot be justified on any ground. It repeats an earlier mistake. Sheltering armed groups that other country regards as a mortal threat has once again put Afghanistan on a collision course. Pakistan's response was a strike in Kabul in October 2025 and a sustained air campaign from February 2026, making force a main tool of interaction.

Yet force has not brought security, and confrontation is a course neither country can sustain for long. The strongest argument for peace is not sentimental. It is arithmetic.

Afghanistan is landlocked, and Pakistan offers it some of the shortest routes to the Arabian Sea. Bilateral trade reached nearly $2 billion in FY2024-25 despite political friction. Pakistan, for its part, needs a land route to Central Asia, and Afghanistan is the natural one. Projects such as the Trans-Afghan Railway, CASA-1000 and TAPI are meant to link Central Asia's energy and markets with South Asia. All of them pass through this one border.

Conflict already carries a cost that does not show up on the battlefield. Afghan traders have moved towards Iran and Central Asia after repeated closures of routes through Pakistan, and Afghanistan's total trade actually grew in 2025 as they did so. Pakistan is exploring alternative access to Central Asia through China and Iran. This should worry both governments. Once traders build new supply chains, they rarely return simply because the politics improve. Every prolonged closure moves a share of commerce away, possibly for good.

There is a deeper change required in Kabul. Afghanistan's celebrated resistance to foreign domination has been central to its national memory. But resistance is an instrument of survival, not a model of governance. A society cannot permanently organise itself around the virtues needed to defeat invaders. The qualities that win a war, such as secrecy, hierarchy, ideological rigidity and suspicion, are not necessarily those needed to build universities, run cities, attract investment, educate women and men, negotiate trade agreements and take part confidently in the modern economy. The move from insurgency to government demands an intellectual transition as profound as the military victory that preceded it.

Restraining the TTP is therefore a matter of sovereignty and self-interest, not a favour to Pakistan. A government that hosts groups attacking its largest neighbour will find it hard to attract the capital its economy needs.

Pakistan has its own homework. Geography does not translate into permanent influence and on the expectation that past support buys present.

That is where a new relationship could begin. The two states do not need to agree about everything. France and Germany did not erase their wars before building Europe. Southeast Asian states did not settle every territorial disagreement before building economic cooperation. Successful regions are not composed of countries without historical grievances. They are often composed of countries that eventually decide that prosperity is a more productive use of geography than revenge.

Pakistan and Afghanistan face precisely that choice. One road leads towards an increasingly militarised frontier, alternative trade routes, proxy accusations, radicalisation and generations taught to regard the people across the border as adversaries. The other turns the same geography into corridors: Karachi and Gwadar connected northward, Kabul connected southward, Central Asian energy flowing towards South Asia, and families, traders and students crossing a border regulated by states rather than militants.

The mountain passes will remain whichever road is chosen. So will the Durand Line, Pakistan and Afghanistan. That is the lesson both countries have taken too long to learn: you can choose your policies, allies and governments, but not your neighbour.

Sometimes the most useful act available to societies accustomed to conflict is not to win another battle. It is to turn the page.

title: Makkah moment
author: none@none.com (Fahd Humayun)
content:
THERE is no disputing that the coming together of Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye comes at a critical juncture for West Asia, even if several aspects around the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement’s precise operationalisation remain unclear.
There are good reasons for Islamabad to view this as a significant strategic opportunity. The arrangement, forged in the shadow of the US and Israeli war on Iran, responds to a growing imperative for regional stakeholders to exercise greater control in stabilising a region fractured by conflict. It also builds on long-standing relationships between three important middle powers whose security is bound up in regional outcomes. Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have decades of military and diplomatic cooperation behind them. Turkiye has important extensive defence ties with both. With US retrenchment from the region increasingly appearing inevitable, institutionalising these relationships offers some much-needed strategic coherence to a region beset by complex challenges.
But for Pakistan to make the most of this moment — and for it to translate the compact into lasting strategic advantage — several caveats deserve consideration.
First, for this ‘non-directional’ arrangement to truly be regionally tenable, it must avoid becoming a source of further division in the Middle East. For Pakistan, the present crisis involving Ansarullah (the Houthis) in the Red Sea offers an early test of whether the alliance can resist being drawn into the region’s existing rivalries. There is no disputing the fact that the stability of the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia matters enormously to Pakistan: it is an important source of energy and financial support, and home to a large Pakistani diaspora whose remittances contribute significantly to foreign exchange earnings.
The strategic opportunity comes with caveats.
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz has also dramatically increased Pakistan’s dependency on the flow of oil through the Red Sea. But direct military involvement against the Houthis does risk drawing the alliance deeper into existing regional rivalries, risking Islamabad’s position with Tehran, and testing Pakistan’s stated policy commitment to avoiding camp politics. Ultimately, Pakistan’s usefulness to the alliance might lie in its ability to exploit the diplomatic space it retains with both Tehran and Riyadh, using those channels to encourage dialogue and de-escalation.
Second, in terms of objectives, military coordination, defence-industrial cooperation and, ultimately, collective defence are not incompatible with one another. But it is that final commitment, however, that will require the most careful thinking about where Pakistan’s obligations to the other two countries begin and end. A decade ago, in 2015, Pakistan’s parliament played an important role in the decision not to commit Pakistani troops to the Saudi-led war in Yemen. While the intervening decade has arguably seen an erosion of Pakistan’s democratic institutions, the country’s leaders must still remember that major commitments abroad still require political dialogue and consensus at home, not least given the country’s demographic diversity and the ability of external security choices to reverberate internally.
Finally, and relatedly, those shaping Pakistan’s strategic direction would be wise to recognise that Pakistan’s expanding strategic horizons cannot be divorced from the pressures it confronts at home and that while there is no arguing that regional influence can be an asset, it is important to build the domestic capacity to sustain. At present, Pakistan confronts a serious trifecta of terrorism, political instability and persistent economic fr­­agility. This year has been among Pakis­tan’s deadliest for terrorism in recent memory. Fraught go­­vernance challe­nges in KP and Ba­­lochistan add to that insecurity. For a country already contending with multiple sources of instability at home, expanding commitments abroad without thought to improved governance and/or a corresponding domestic reset at home risks weakening the very foundations on which any newfound regional influence must ultimately rest.
None of these caveats detracts from the rare opportunity Makkah presents. In the shadow of looming threats from India and Afghanistan, and general instability unleashed by America’s war in Iran, the arrangement offers Pakistan the chance to do several things: to extract strategic currency from its military capacity, to expand defence-industrial cooperation with important partners, and to eventually be a consequential voice in shaping whatever security architecture emerges from the ashes of the US war against Iran. But these things also require more than aspiration. For Islamabad, that means navigating existing regional fault lines and developing a better political compact at home.
The writer is assistant professor of political science, Tufts University.

For the alliance to be successful and for Pakistan to benefit, it must avoid exacerbating existing regional rivalries (e.g., Red Sea conflict) and carefully define its collective defence obligations.

title: When the state becomes an obstacle
author: none@none.com (Fayyaz Ahmad Khan)
content:
THE Federal Investigation Agency recently busted what it describes as an alleged network involved in fake apostille stickers and official stamps, booking 22 suspects, including six officials of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The investigation will establish what happened and who was responsible. But there is a larger question that should concern all of us: why does obtaining a perfectly legitimate government service become so difficult that an ecosystem of agents and middlemen can flourish around it?
Anatol Lieven offered an uncomfortable explanation more than a decade ago in Pakistan: A Hard Country. Writing about Pakistan’s bureaucracy, he observed that “The bureaucracy acts as an agency of distributing patronage rather than good government”. He was making a broader point than simply accusing officials of corruption: formal institutions themselves can be shaped by patronage, personal relationships and competing interests.
The result is a paradox. The machinery of the state can be weak and dysfunctional, yet the networks around it can make the system remarkably resilient. Those same networks, however, can make the state harder for ordinary citizens to navigate. Lieven’s observation remains relevant because the problem citizens encounter today is not simply corruption. It is the growing difficulty of dealing with the state itself.
Getting a document attested from the foreign affairs ministry can mean hours in queues, repeated visits, uncertainty about requirements and the possibility of another objection from another official. When a legitimate administrative process becomes sufficiently difficult, the middleman finds an opportunity. And when the middleman becomes almost indispensable, corruption has fertile ground in which to grow.
The answer to every administrative failure cannot be another layer of control.
I know something about this from personal experience. Last year, I wrote to the foreign minister, Ishaq Dar, about the immense difficulties you­ng Pakistanis were facing in getting documents attested. I asked for a system that would allow citizens to obtain a legitimate government service with dignity, without spending hours standing in the heat or cold. The response was brief: the authorities were aware of the problem and had already taken steps to improve the situation.
Unfortunately, my experience since then suggests that the problem has not disappeared.
My own family has encountered similar problems elsewhere in the system. Two adult daughters were once stopped at Lahore airport and questioned for almost two hours before an international trip, including being asked why they were travelling without a male relative.
On another occasion, the Foreign Office refused to attest an affidavit prepared for a university abroad because, I was told, both parents had to consent even though the applicant was an adult. The embassy of the country concerned eventually accepted the affidavit without the Foreign Office attestation.
More recently, a newborn’s passport became another bureaucratic journey. The father, living abroad, had to fly back to Pakistan because his presence was considered necessary before the passport could be issued. Even after the passport was processed, the parents were asked to have their identity documents attested by a Grade-17 officer before collection. These are not extraordinary demands in a country facing war or famine. They concern passports, affidavits and identity documents.
And that is the point. A state does not become stronger by making every legitimate interaction with it more difficult. Nor does every additional verification, signature, attestation or layer of authority necessarily make a system more secure. Sometimes it simply creates another point at which a citizen becomes dependent on an official’s discretion.
We often discuss corruption as though it begins with the person offering money at a counter. But the deeper problem can begin much earlier, when the legitimate route becomes so cumbersome that people start looking for another route.
Lieven’s insight was that the problem is not simply individual dishonesty. It is the way the system itself can operate through patronage, personal rel­a­­tionships and discretion. As he put it, people with even limited power can use it to “turn to their ad­­vantage the workings of the law and the bureaucracy”.
That is why the answer to every administrative failure cannot be another layer of control. A new verification may be introduced to prevent fraud. Another signature may be demanded in the name of security. Another attestation may be added to ensure authenticity. Each may appear reasonable in isolation. Together, they can create a maze in which the honest citizen becomes increasingly dependent on the very system that is supposed to serve them.
Pakistan is a poor country. Its citizens understand that. They do not expect government offices to provide five-star service. But they can reasonably expect something much more basic: when the law gives them a legitimate right, the state should make it reasonably easy to exercise that right. This is the argument I had made in my letter to the foreign minister a year back.
A birth certificate should not become an odyssey. A passport should not require unnecessary suspicion. A document attestation should not require an agent. A citizen should not have to prove, at every counter, that he or she is innocent of some imagined wrongdoing.
The government does not need another committee to discover this. It needs to look at the citizen’s journey through the system and ask a simple question: how many of these steps are actually necessary?
Because corruption is not created only at the counter. Sometimes the conditions for it are created much earlier, by a system that makes a simple, legitimate service unnecessarily difficult.
The writer is a former journalist and strategic communication and public health professional, with experience across Asia, Africa and the Middle East.

title: The unholy alliance
author: none@none.com (Zahid Hussain)
content:
THE Israeli prime minister’s reported secret visit to Abu Dhabi last Sunday has reinforced the growing nexus between the UAE and the Zionist state. It was not the first time that Benjamin Netanyahu had made an unannounced trip to the Gulf country. In March this year, at the height of the Iran war, he travelled there to meet UAE President Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed al-Nahyan.
During the same period, the head of Mossad, Israel’s main intelligence agency, made two trips to the country to apparently coordinate military operations. And last week, while 77 nations boycotted the Israeli prime minister’s speech at the UN General Assembly, the UAE delegation remained seated — a clear show of solidarity with the Zionist state.
Since joining the Abraham Accords in 2020, the UAE has not only established diplomatic relations with Israel but has gone much further, elevating the relationship into a de facto alliance — even as the Israeli state was carrying out a genocidal war in Gaza. That relationship deepened as the US, along with Israel, imposed an unprovoked war on Iran.
The extraordinary relationship between the two countries marks a developing unholy alliance in a rapidly changing regional order, as America’s war on Iran drags on. The UAE has reportedly carried out its own strikes on Iran and has also borne the brunt of retaliatory strikes — with devastating effect — despite the deployment of the Iron Dome air defence system, run by Israeli military personnel.
Its close military cooperation with Israel has drawn the UAE directly into the war on Iran.
It is the first time this highly advanced system has been deployed outside Israel and the US, signalling the critical role of the Emirates in a potential Israeli-led regional defence alliance. It is also the first Arab-Israeli relationship to acquire real military and industrial substance. And this Israel-UAE nexus goes beyond the ongoing Iran war: the UAE appears to be a critical part of Israel’s plan to build what Netanyahu calls the “hexagon of alliances”.
That idea was pitched by the Israeli prime minister early this year. Speaking at a cabinet meeting on Feb 22, 2026, days before the visit of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Netanyahu presented his vision of creating “a hexagon of alliances around or within the Middle East” — a bloc against what he described as the “radical Shia and emerging Sunni axis”. He named four members — Israel, India, Greece and Cyprus — and left the remaining slots (Arab, African and Asian states) unnamed. But it is widely assumed that the Emirates is one of the six, given its close diplomatic and defence ties with Israel.
Netanyahu also pointed to intelligence-sharing and counterterrorism cooperation with India as the core of the project. Modi’s February visit produced a Special Strategic Partnership between the two countries, which have long cooperated on defence and intelligence. Israel is one of India’s largest arms suppliers. The UAE, too, has built close defence ties with New Delhi. All three are part of the four-nation I2U2 grouping, alongside the US, and of IMEC, the India-Middle East-Europe Economic Corridor. This web of alliances, bound together by bilateral defence relationships, is shaping the emerging security landscape in West Asia and beyond.
Although the Israeli-proposed hexagon alliance has not yet taken formal shape, it is widely seen as a potential counter to the Makkah alliance — which Israel portrays, wrongly, as a ‘Sunni alliance’. Netanyahu has repeatedly called Turkiye a greater threat than Iran and a major challenge to his ‘Greater Israel’ ambition. Against this background, the growing Israel-UAE diplomatic and defence cooperation is alarming.
Over the past few years, the UAE has drifted away from its Gulf allies on a range of regional and foreign policy issues, above all by widening its differences with Saudi Arabia. The Emirates is accused of arming and financing a separatist group in strife-torn southern Yemen, bringing the UAE into conflict with Riyadh. It is also widely believed to be arming and funding an armed group involved in Sudan’s civil war, one accused of mass atrocities. And it backs Somaliland, a breakaway region of Somalia recognised only by Israel — while every other Arab state supports a united Somalia.
A few months ago, at the height of the Iran war, the Emirates pulled out of Opec, the Saudi-led oil cartel, severely damaging the organisation. Its close military cooperation with Israel has drawn the Emirates directly into the war on Iran, endangering its own security in the process. Any participation in an Israeli-proposed alliance could prove extremely destabilising for the region.
Pakistan’s own relations with the Emirates have hit a low over the past few years. Early this year, the UAE withdrew a $3 billion deposit from the State Bank of Pakistan, and once-close ties have become significantly strained. With a large Pakistani workforce in the Emirates, the shift has put Pakistan in a very difficult position, which requires a delicate balancing act.
The widening regional divide — in the middle of the Iran war, Israel’s continuing genocide in Gaza and its military actions in Lebanon — is extremely troubling. Israel’s idea of a ‘hexagon alliance’ that also includes India is dangerous for Pakistan’s security, particularly as Israel and India are already tied in a strategic relationship.
It is certainly not good news for the Middle East and the wider region, which is being rocked by America’s unending war on Iran. The situation has become much more complicated with the escalating conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthi rebels in Yemen.
Last week, the military chiefs of the three allied countries met to discuss the deteriorating situation, and there is talk that Article 5 of the alliance — under which an attack on one member is considered an attack on all — could be activated. Any such move could draw Pakistan directly into the conflict. With a resolution to the Iran war still far off, an expansion of the conflict could render the situation far more explosive. Against this backdrop, the unholy alliance between Israel and the UAE could further destabilise the region, with far-reaching implications.
The writer is an author and journalist.

title: Trump-Xi summit
author: none@none.com (Mahir Ali)
content:
ONE of the few revelations that emerged from last week’s Sino-US summit in Washington is that President Xi Jinping is “an expert on stone, aside from many other things, and he loves good granite”. At least that was the host’s verdict after the esteemed guest was obliged to examine the new White House helipad and the Marine One copter in which Donald Trump flits about. Xi’s reflections on the ordeal are unlikely ever to be revealed but, whether or not he’s actually a fan of granite, we do know that he’s an expert at being stony-faced — a feat that his American host, among many others, is incapable of emulating.
More seriously, though, it’s somewhat gratifying to see the top honchos of the world’s biggest military and economic powers playing footsie with one another. Trump’s first presidential campaign a decade ago was grounded in relentless hostility to China, and he has blamed the 2020 election outcome partly on Beijing’s interference — which is as absurd as his adversaries crediting Russia with the 2016 result. Noticeably, that plaint wasn’t revisited last week.
There was no joint statement at the end of what both sides officially declared to be a huge success. But whereas the mainstream Western liberal media has generally been unduly sceptical about specific achievements, Chinese state media has been celebrating the win-win accomplishments in platitudinous terms, such as “working in the same direction” and “respect, fairness and reciprocity”. That is vaguely reassuring, even though nothing is guaranteed. AI wasn’t ignored, but the scope for future discussions remains uncertain.
A decade ago, in one of his last documentaries, The Coming War on China, John Pilger laid out the prospects of an operation in the making since the 1950s. He focused in part on Bikini Atoll in the colonised Marshall Islands as a site where hydrogen bombs were regularly tested, with little concern for the inhabitants, in the quest for Asia-Pacific domination. Many decades later, the “pivot to Asia” was essentially part of the same pattern.
There is much that China and the US appear not to have discussed.
‘Who lost China?’ was a key factor in the purge of State Department officials who correctly predicted the Maoist takeover in 1949, which led to the Formosa ‘crisis’ that remains unresolved. Trump does not appear to be too concerned about what becomes of Taiwan and has thus far held back on supplying new arms to the island. Any future war over Taiwan would be both stupid and globally disastrous. But can it be avoided? That’s a question for an indeterminate future. Pakistan, like several other nations, has relied on both China and the US for decades. This is likely to continue. The perception of Beijing as an all-seasons saviour flows into a different challenge. What comes next might come as a surprise.
The difference between the US and China is that the former is floundering, while the latter, for all its flaws and tribulations, retains its edge. There is no guarantee that the US and China will remain on close terms for the remainder of the year, never mind the forthcoming APEC and G20 gatherings. Whatever Xi’s Washington ordeal might have accomplished, the US and China remain at loggerheads in various respects, and the possibility of a war cannot entirely be discounted. The consequences of such an eventuality are too horrible to imagine. Xi’s reception in the US has been seen as an unusual accomplishment. What does not necessarily follow is superpower bonhomie, despite the likelihood of two more Xi-Trump encounters before the year is out.
Whether the envisaged progress can be taken at face value is an open question. Le­­a­­ving AI aside, there is much else that China and the US ap­­pear not to have discussed. The pron­o­u­­n­cements from Beijing have broadly been more positive than the American pronouncements. Neither side, though, has offered clarity about what lies ahead. Neither technology nor Taiwan may be enough to persuade Trump to challenge China, but the post-Trump scenario remains hazy.
A US-China conflagration is unlikely but cannot be dismissed out of hand. As long as both sides see each other as adversaries, the prospect of eventual hostilities cannot entirely be discounted. Such hostilities would be a multifaceted disaster.
China has not stood out as a consequential opponent of the genocide in Palestine. Nor has it directly participated in Iran’s resistance to the US-Israeli onslaught, despite allegations about shared intelligence. China cannot be excluded from West Asia, but it has largely been silent about the genocide in Gaza and the West Bank. Precisely what kind of role China wishes to play in the region is unclear. Yet, notwithstanding the evidently meagre accomplishments of the summit, even the slightest hope of superpower rapprochement deser­ves to be embraced as a triumph of hope.

title: A bailout state?
author: none@none.com (Dr Niaz Murtaza)
content:
THE country’s external liquidity rests shakily on the two crutches of endless IMF loans and rollovers of patron-state deposits. Both carry high costs — economic and political.
Our rulers entice patron states to bankroll a near-bankrupt state via its geopolitical, not economic, value. Rulers exploit both for personal, not public, gains. They court patrons well, but turn patronage into public progress poorly and personal profits ably. So, our growth spurts are all import-led rather than export-led. We spend dollars faster than we earn and court crises. We recover by choking growth instead of increasing it alongside exports. We have had several chances but have squandered most of them.
Musharraf squandered the biggest one this century. He ruled the longest, with the deep state and opposition under his thumb, and gained over $45bn in US aid, debt relief, FDI, and portfolio inflows after 9/11. Yet, a strong export base eluded him. Inflows fuelled consumption, imports, and property binges and bubbles; volatile portfolio funds and domestically focused FDI later led to outflows. They initially kept the rupee high, hurting exports. Their value doubled, but value-added dawdled and the export-GDP ratio fell below 1990s levels. A record current account deficit of 8.2 per cent of GDP in 2008 led to a big crisis. Bad security policies fuelled two conflicts that still hurt progress. The PPP cut the deficit. But energy woes, insecurity, ineptitude and failed reforms reduced growth.
Later, CPEC provided over $20 billion for energy and roads. This eased energy gaps, but the PML-N failed to build a durable export base. An expensive rupee led to an import surge and a current account deficit of about 6pc by 2018. The PTI had brought it down to 0.6pc by 2021 and managed the Covid phase well. But the Covid stimulus raised imports as exports lagged. The deficit rose to 4.6pc in 2022, partly due to global price shocks and political turmoil. So, the PML-N bequeathed a crisis to the PTI only to inherit one back, karma-style.
We spend dollars faster than we earn and court crises.
Import-led growth led to dollar crunches. Instead of curbing crises, high reserves made them more likely as rulers increased imports to fuel growth. Their frequency and common causes could have taught the current rulers how to avert such crises. But they are as clueless about them as they are about regular floods, even though such crises can be foreseen and forestalled. This is worse than incompetence; it shows wilful neglect. They cause and gain from such crises. The people are worse off now.
As CPEC flows shrank, we courted IMF loans and state deposits, which ballooned from 36pc of the State Bank’s reserves in 2016, when deposits were only $700 million, to nearly 600pc in early 2023. About $11bn in IMF debt, $8bn in Saudi deposits and $4bn in Chinese deposits together still exceed even our highest-ever SBP reserves of $21bn. We are the most persistent user of both crutches over time, and we now have the second-most such deposits and the third-most IMF debt globally. They are on top of an external debt of over $80bn. Unlike that debt, they don’t fund projects or jobs directly, earn no direct revenue to pay the interest and are taken only due to a dollar crunch. Even these crutches may not carry the weight of our follies, so we now eye a $10bn lifeline from our oldest but most fickle patron — the US. Bangladesh, once our lesser half, has no such deposits, and its IMF debt is only 13pc of reserves as its $48bn exports mock our $30bn levels.
Such crutches hurt. The PML-N and PTI both ignited growth spurts as reserves peaked. Despite hi­­g­her SBP reserves now, this set-up hasn’t cha­nged outcomes, given the nature of its rese­rve cushion. The IMF keeps us on a leash, and patron-state de­­posits can be recalled quickly (as in the UAE case), unlike flows with longer, fi­_xed return dates. So, even patronage quality has fallen: from post-9/11 aid and debt relief to CPEC flows to harsh loans and fickle deposits. We now build reserves precariously rather than finance them prudently or earn them creatively.
After four years, this set-up boasts only stabilisation and opaque foreign forays. But as a strong export base and growth elude it, stabilisation is really stagnation. Foreign forays are sucking us into endless wars, jeopardising our own security for the sake of others. We face two risky paths: hobble on with slow growth and risk unrest, or rush recklessly into import-led growth to court a dollar crisis and unrest. With no major investments here even from the patrons it serves loyally, only the two crutches prop up a bailout state. How long will its weak life jackets keep it afloat?
The writer has a PhD in political economy from the University of California, Berkeley, and 25 years of grassroots-to-senior-level experience across 50 countries.

title: Security-development nexus
author: none@none.com (Ishrat Husain)
content:
PAKISTAN can’t achieve sustained economic growth by treating security as a separate problem for the security apparatus to handle while econom­ists focus on investment, exports, productivity and fiscal reform. Insecurity destroys the very conditions on which economic development depe­nds, while development strengthens the foundations of security. Our crisis makes this nexus impossible to ignore. For decades, discussions on investment, production, growth, and development have largely focused on economic policies while underestimating the non-economic environment in which they operate. Yet, security of life and property, political stability, rule of law, judicial independence, federal-provincial coordination, accountability, and regional peace directly affect economic outcomes. Unless these improve, returns from economic reforms will remain below potential.
Increasing militancy and Pakistan’s top position on the Global Terrorism Index 2026 are damaging lives and economic prospects. The recent attack on a police compound in Kohat, in which 37 people, including military personnel, were killed, received international coverage. Foreign business people and executives reportedly cancelled plan­ned visits, while travel advisories issued by sever­al governments can discourage their nationals from visiting Pakistan. In 2025, TTP attacks in KP and BLA strikes in Balochistan caused hundreds of ca­­sualties among security personnel. The past decade’s trend shows that terrorism is no longer episodic. It is a structural constraint on investment, trade, tourism, development and employment.
The origins of the TTP challenge go back several decades. Pakistan’s decision in the 1980s to align with the US in opposing the Soviet occupation of Afghanistan had consequences beyond the immediate strategic goal. The proliferation of arms and drugs, sectarian violence, growth of militant groups and the spread of extremist ideologies created a social and institutional environment that facilitated terrorism in Pakistan.
After the Soviets left Afghanistan, Pakistan became involved in efforts to shape a political settlement among Afghan factions. The failure of power-sharing arrangements and the ensuing civil war led to the emergence of the Taliban, who captured Kabul in 1996. Pakistan supported their regime. But 9/11 fundamentally altered the situation. Pakistan joined the global campaign against terrorism, itself becoming a major target. When the US decided to leave Afghanistan, Pakistan played an important role in the Doha process. The Ashraf Ghani government’s collapse in 2021 and the Taliban’s return led to expectations that cross-border terrorism would decline. Instead, the TTP, now equipped with modern weapons left behind by Nato forces, intensified their attacks.
The challenge is to build security through development, and development through security.
Diplomatic efforts involving China, Saudi Arabia and Türkiye have not produced a durable solution. Insecurity along the western frontier has disrupted bilateral trade, imposing costs on manufacturers, traders and transport operators, especially in KP and Balochistan. Security and commerce are now directly linked. Balochistan poses a different but equally serious challenge. It has seen a sharp escalation in asymmetric warfare and insurgency. Highways, railways, bridges, gas pipelines, electricity transmission lines, and other infrastructure have been targeted. Mine workers, labourers from other provinces and government officials have been attacked or abducted. In places, the state’s administrative presence and writ have been weakened.
The economic consequences are immediate. Chi­­nese nationals and companies in Pakistan need extensive security. Attacks on Chinese citizens in Karachi, Dasu and elsewhere have led to concerns in Beijing and slowed some CPEC-related activities. Gwadar’s industrial potential remains largely unrealised, partly because Chinese companies are reluctant to deploy personnel in insecure conditions. An industrial zone won’t flourish when investors can’t operate confidently.
Security operations alone can’t resolve Balochistan’s problem. Kinetic action is necessary against militants but must be accompanied by development. Balochistan suffers from serious deficits in education, health, clean water, infrastructure, employment and private investment. When economic opportunities are few, grievances become a source of recruitment for insurgent groups. So the province needs not just security spending but also a development strategy to create jobs, boost local institutions, and ensure communities see tangible benefits from Balochistan’s natural resources and strategic location. Regional instability adds to the problem. Disruption of trade with Iran and closure or restriction of border crossings such as Chaman have hurt exporters and communities that rely on cross-border commerce. Clearly, peace is not just a diplomatic aim; it is an economic asset.
Pakistan must use its diplomatic capital to promote regional economic integration. Better ties with Afghanistan, structured dialogue with India, stable relations with Iran, and expanded links with Central Asian states can enlarge its economic space. Afghanistan, Iran, north India, and Central Asia can be important markets for Pakistani goods and services. Gwadar could become a transshipment and logistics gateway for landlocked Central Asian economies, generating transit revenues and creating opportunities for Pakistani exporters. Uzbekistan, Kyrgyzstan and Tajikistan offer markets that Pakistan has so far penetrated modestly. Regional connectivity can revive projects such as the Iran-Pakistan gas pipeline, TAPI, and CASA, subject to their political, financial, commercial, and security feasibility.
Greater regional trade will create demand for transport, logistics, warehousing, banking, insurance, IT and manufacturing. It will create jobs and give border communities greater economic sta­­ke in stability. None of this means that economic reforms should wait for peace. Quite the contrary. Fiscal reform, energy sector restructuring, taxation, deregulation, privatisation, export diversification, human capital development and institutional reform must continue uninterrupted. But they must be supported by steps that reduce the security premium imposed on economic activity.
Security and development are two sides of the same national strategy. Insecurity raises transaction costs, discourages investment, destroys infrastructure, disrupts trade, deters foreign personnel and limits employment. Lack of economic opportunity, weak institutions and regional isolation can deepen the conditions in which insecurity flourishes. The goal should be to create an economy in which security, development and opportunity reinforce each other. Military capability can suppress threats. But only sustained economic development, effective institutions, political stability and regional peace can remove many of the conditions that allow those threats to regenerate.
Our choice is not between security and development. The challenge is to build security through development, and development through security. Until that nexus becomes the organising principle of policy, economic reforms will operate below their potential and Pakistan will remain vulnerable to cycles of instability, low investment and weak growth.
The writer is a former State Bank governor.

title: Watching the glaciers
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE latest signs from Pakistan’s mountains are worrying. Suparco says the number of unfrozen glacial lakes it observed rose from 40 in early July to 105 in August, while some were larger than previously recorded. Not every thawing lake poses the same danger. But when a lake grows unusually large, it can put greater pressure on the loose rock and debris holding back its waters, increasing the risk of a glacial lake outburst flood. Hence, satellite monitoring is invaluable, particularly in remote mountain areas. Yet it can only tell part of the story. To know how dangerous a lake really is, experts also need information about its depth, the strength of the natural barrier around it, the condition of nearby glaciers and local weather patterns. Hanging glaciers, which can suddenly collapse and send ice or debris into a lake, present another danger that cannot always be properly understood from satellite images alone. Cloud cover can also obscure the view, as Suparco itself has noted. Pakistan must, therefore, move beyond simply counting and mapping glacial lakes. It needs to know which ones pose the greatest threat, and why.
This means connecting what is seen from space with what scientists find on the ground. When satellite images show a lake expanding rapidly, it should lead to closer field checks involving Suparco, Wapda, universities, meteorological experts and the provincial disaster authorities. Their findings should be brought together in one system showing which lakes are growing, which natural barriers may be weakening, and which villages, roads or other infrastructure lie downstream. Experts have warned that agencies often work separately and that important information about glaciers and local conditions remains missing. With more than 13,000 glaciers, Pakistan cannot study each one in equal detail. Nor does it need to. Satellite monitoring can help identify the lakes that deserve the closest attention, allowing limited scientific resources to be used where the danger is greatest. The jump from 40 to 105 unfrozen lakes should, therefore, be seen as more than another warning about climate change. It is also a test of whether Pakistan can turn the information it already has into practical knowledge — and use that knowledge before a dangerous lake becomes a disaster.

title: TTP: a threat until it is not!
author: M Zeb Khan
content:
The bloodshed in Khyber-Pakhtunkhwa is becoming horrifyingly familiar. In September alone, we witnessed with shock two devastating blasts in K-P which killed police personnel and civilians and left scores injured. The attackers used an explosives-laden vehicle before armed militants stormed the compound. It was not an isolated incident but another entry in a growing catalogue of violence stretching across North Waziristan, Bannu, Lakki Marwat, Tank, Hangu, and beyond.

The obvious question is no longer whether Pakistan possesses the capacity to confront terrorism. It does. Pakistan has sophisticated weapons systems, one of the world's largest professional armies, extensive intelligence organisations, and decades of counterterrorism experience. Yet relatively small militant organisations continue to kill policemen, soldiers and civilians almost at will where and when they choose! This is the paradox Pakistan must confront.

The TTP and associated militant networks do not need to defeat the Pakistani military. They merely need to survive it. An insurgent chooses when to attack, where to disappear and when not to fight. Motivation, mobility, local networks and sanctuary can compensate for extraordinary disparities in conventional military power. And the threat is evolving. The Express Tribune recently reported that militants in K-P are increasingly employing drones, thermal imaging and night-vision technology. Some 156 police personnel were killed in militant attacks during the first seven months of 2026 alone.

So, describing these organisations simply as ragtag bands risks misunderstanding the problem. Their material resources may be tiny compared with those of the state but their ability to adapt should not be underestimated. Pakistan's real difficulty appears elsewhere: consistency of purpose. The country has repeatedly demonstrated that it possesses the military will to confront militants. But military success and strategic success are not synonymous. Terrorists can be removed from a valley today and return tomorrow if intelligence, policing, prosecution, border management, governance and economic opportunity do not fill the space they leave behind. Military operations can suppress an insurgency; they cannot, by themselves, eliminate the ecosystem that reproduces it. That was precisely the insight behind the National Action Plan formulated after the horrific APS massacre. NAP recognised that terrorism required far more than battlefield operations.

The tragedy is not that Pakistan lacked a strategy. It is that implementation repeatedly lagged behind declaration. An equally damaging ambiguity arose from differentiating between militants considered immediately hostile to Pakistan and those whose activities were directed elsewhere. Whatever tactical logic once supported distinctions between so-called "good" and "bad" militants, the experience of subsequent years illustrates their danger. Militant ecosystems are porous. Fighters move, alliances shift, ideologies overlap and yesterday's good can turn bad tomorrow.

There must therefore be one uncomplicated principle: no armed non-state organisation should be permitted to operate outside the law. The Afghan dimension makes the challenge still more serious. A UN monitoring report released in 2026 described the TTP as one of the largest terrorist groups operating in Afghanistan and reported that it had been afforded greater liberty and support there.

Pakistan consequently faces both a domestic counterterrorism challenge and a difficult diplomatic-security problem across its western border. Yet strategic clarity should not mean indiscriminate force. A sophisticated state must distinguish between terrorist leadership, operational fighters, facilitators, sympathisers and people who can genuinely abandon militancy. IBOs, prosecution and reintegration can operate simultaneously.

The fundamental question is not whether Pakistan is powerful enough to defeat terrorism. It is whether that power can be translated into sustained political will, institutional coordination and strategic consistency. Militants do not have to become stronger than the state to threaten it. They only have to survive in the spaces where the state is inconsistent.

whyMatters: This article critically analyzes the enduring threat posed by the TTP despite Pakistan's military capabilities, highlighting crucial gaps in strategic consistency and policy implementation. Aspirants can leverage its arguments to provide nuanced analysis on internal security, national action plans, and the complexities of counter-insurgency for essay and current affairs papers.
summary: Despite possessing significant military capacity, Pakistan faces a paradox where relatively small militant organizations like the TTP continue to operate effectively, demonstrating a gap between military power and strategic success.

The TTP and associated networks survive by exploiting state inconsistencies, adapting technology (drones, night vision), and leveraging mobility, local networks, and sanctuaries, rather than by directly defeating the military.

The National Action Plan (NAP) correctly identified the need for a comprehensive approach beyond battlefield operations, but its implementation repeatedly lagged, and the distinction between 'good' and 'bad' militants proved to be a damaging ambiguity.

The Afghan dimension complicates the challenge, with the TTP reportedly gaining greater liberty and support there, underscoring the necessity for a clear principle of 'no armed non-state organization' within the law.

Strategic success against terrorism requires sustained political will, institutional coordination, and consistency across intelligence, policing, prosecution, border management, governance, and economic opportunity, rather than solely military operations.
