title: Climate neutral
author: none@none.com (Aisha Khan)
content:
SOUTH Asia has long viewed peace through the familiar language of power: territory, armies, missiles, borders, alliances and economic weight. China, India, Pakistan and Bangladesh sit at different points on this spectrum, and their relative capabilities are often measured in GDP, reserves, industrial capacity, defence budgets, troop strength, air power and nuclear weapons. Yet the recent climate- induced disaster in Nepal has introduced another measure of power, one that does not respect borders and cannot be deterred by military superiority. It is the capacity of a state to absorb shock, protect its people, maintain essential services and recover without falling into political or economic crisis.
Seen through that lens, the region’s strategic map looks very different. China possesses an enormous economy, deep industrial capacity, extensive infrastructure and one of the world’s largest and most technologically advanced militaries. India combines a huge and rapidly growing economy with a large military, a nuclear arsenal, substantial manpower and an expanding industrial and technological base. Pakistan has considerable military capability, including nuclear weapons and a large standing force, but a smaller economy and tighter fiscal space. Bangladesh has a much smaller military and economic base, yet its experience with cyclones, floods, early-warning systems and community adaptation demonstrates that resilience is not simply a function of national wealth or firepower.
The contrast is important. Military power is designed principally to impose costs on an adversary or prevent an adversary from doing so. Economic power provides resources to sustain that effort. Climate resilience performs a different function: it reduces the number of occasions on which societies are pushed into crisis in the first place.
This matters because South Asia is unusually exposed to climate shocks. The monsoon is the region’s economic and ecological lifeline, while the Himalayas, great river systems, densely populated plains and low-lying coasts connect the fates of countries that frequently disagree on almost everything else. The World Bank estimates that more than half of South Asians have been affected by a natural disaster in the past two decades and climate change can turn economic strength into a temporary illusion. This distinction should reshape the meaning of security in South Asia. Climate stress can make confrontations more dangerous by weakening economies, intensifying competition over water and food, increasing displacement and narrowing governments’ room for manoeuvre.
Defence must acquire another layer that protects from climate risks.
The paradox is striking. States may spend billions acquiring weapons to prepare for threats that might never materialise while underinvesting in systems designed for disasters that are already occurring. Climate change is therefore like a progressively crippling disease. It does not ask whether a country is rich or poor, democratic or authoritarian, nuclear-armed or defenceless. It attacks the physical foundations on which every form of national power rests and undermines systems that support life.
The lesson is not that armies are irrelevant. States still need credible defence, and deterrence remains essential in a region marked by unresolved disputes. The lesson is that defence must acquire another layer that protects from climate risks. The logic is compelling because climate risks cross borders. The most rational response is therefore neither surrender nor unilateralism, but mutually reinforcing mechanisms in which each country gains more from cooperation than from acting alone.
The future balance of power in South Asia should consequently be measured in two columns. The first will continue to contain GDP, re­­s­e­rves, technology, troop numbers, missiles, aircraft and nuclear capability. The second should contain reservoirs, resilient cities, functioning hospitals, protected crops, reliable grids, emergency communications, early-warning coverage, fiscal buffers and the ability to recover quickly from catastrophe. The first column determines how much damage a state can threaten or withstand in war. The second determines whether its people can remain alive and its institutions functional when the enemy is a changing climate.
That is the great neutralising force of climate change. The wisest strategy, therefore, is not to abandon power, but to broaden its definition. South Asia needs layers of defence that reinforce one another: military deterrence, economic resilience, environmental cooperation and human security. Peace will depend not only on preventing countries from fighting each other, but also on helping them survive the common shocks that none can defeat alone.
The writer is a climate policy analyst.
aisha@csccc.org.pk
Published in Dawn, September 22nd, 2026

whyMatters: This article offers a crucial paradigm shift in understanding security, moving beyond traditional military-economic power to emphasize climate resilience, which is highly relevant for Pakistan's vulnerability. summary: Climate change introduces a new measure of state power: the capacity to absorb shocks, protect its people, maintain essential services, and recover from disasters without falling into political or economic crisis.

Traditional metrics of power (military capabilities, economic strength) are insufficient against the borderless and indiscriminate nature of climate shocks; climate resilience is crucial for societal stability.

South Asia's extreme vulnerability to climate shocks, particularly its reliance on the monsoon and shared river systems, makes climate change a critical factor in regional stability and potential conflict over resources like water and food.

Security must be broadened to include defence against climate risks, necessitating environmental cooperation and mutually reinforcing mechanisms among nations to address shared vulnerabilities more effectively than unilateral action.

The monsoon serves as the economic and ecological lifeline for the South Asian region.

title: Autocratic legalism
author: none@none.com (Asad-ul-Mulk)
content:
“THE power of a judicial branch, or of religious authorities who are the custodians of the law, lies only in the legitimacy that they can confer on rulers and in the popular support they receive as protectors of a broad social consensus. Gregory VII could force Henry [IV] to come to Canossa, but he could not actually depose him as emperor,” writes Francis Fukuyama in The Origins of Political Order.
The judiciary has little coercive power to physically thwart excess by the executive. Nevertheless, even against an entrenched executive, there is one power which the judiciary retains. The power to deny the executive, which behaves in an ultra vires manner, the legitimacy it craves. This denial of legitimacy is nontrivial. Writing on the power of corporate groups to impose their will, Max Weber wrote in The Theory of Social and Economic Organisation that “Every such system attempts to establish and to cultivate the belief in its legitimacy”.
North Korea, Equatorial Guinea, Russia, Belarus and Azerbaijan are headed by Kim Jong Un, Teodoro Mbasogo, Vladimir Putin, Alexander Lukashenko and Ilham Aliyev respectively, who are all dictators. Yet all these states hold elections and have legislative bodies and heads of government who exercise executive power in accordance with their respective constitution. Alas, hardly any of these states can be said to harbour true democracy.
A recent paper published in the Journal of Democracy titled ‘How courts undermine democracy’ explains how courts grant to an excessive executive the legitimacy it craves, and perpetuate a cycle of ‘autocratic legalism’. The latter term refers to weaponisation of the law. Prof Kim Lane Scheppele in her essay Autocratic Legalism — published in the University of Chicago Law Review — argues that contemporary autocrats have mastered the use of legal and constitutional methods to weaken democratic institutions, consolidate power and do away with systems of checks and balances.
The courts can deny the executive the legitimacy it wants.
There is a ‘method to the madness’, and recognisable patterns, which enable the weaponisation of the law. Power is first captured through electoral or other means, and paves the way for filling the legislature with stalwarts or cronies. Once the legislature is controlled, it is employed to amend ordinary laws, as well as the constitution, so as to allow for what is called ‘courts capture’, ie, the courts are filled with compliant judges, and any judge who resists is sent home. Sometimes parallel or extraordinary courts, with jurisdiction over and above the existing ones, are established, to disturb and frustrate the legal hierarchy.
With resulting ‘courts capture’, the system of ‘checks and balances’ is effectively dismantled. The heads of constitutional bodies and independent state agencies, which regulate elections, prosecute white collar crime, and survey and indict persons involved in anti-state activities, are replaced with ‘political commissars’. The state’s prosecutorial powers are unleashed on political opponents, and dissenting voices are silenced through legal processes.
The ripples from this reorganisation of the state are so overwhelming that the bureaucracy either capitulates or is shuffled so as to sideline any officer who dares to raise his voice. The media is harnessed as an echo chamber, and thus, total control of the apparatuses of state is ensured.
The doctrine of ‘autocratic legalism’ has the potential to turn judges into instruments of the executive. “Could any court having a discretion in the matter, issue an enforceable writ on the 8, 9 or 10 October against the government that had been brought into existence by the proclamation of presid­e­­nt Iskander Mirza?” asked chief justice Munir in his subsequent writings ru­­minating on ‘The state vs Dosso’ (1958), and cited it as a reason for le­­gitimising the first coup d’état in Pakistan.
Justice Munir’s assessment of the enforceability of the writ, albeit accurate, was an utterly extra-legal consideration, and counterintuitive to his obligation to defend the constitution. The judicial acquiescence conferred legitimacy on a regime that was otherwise wanting.
Resistance by the Supreme Court would not have reined in the usurpers; instead, it would have resulted in the whole court being sent home. Nevertheless, such an act would have denied to the usurpers the legitimacy they crave for, and demonstrated the highest form of judicial sacrifice — seldom extolled — which is pronouncing an unenforceable judgement, even at the peril of giving up one’s exalted office.
Parallel or extraordinary courts, courts capture and amendments to the law and constitution to alter judicial hierarchy and electoral laws, concurrently, are ex-facie facets of ‘autocratic legalism’, and Pakistan ought to be circumspect.
The writer is a practising barrister.

title: Mandate is necessary
author: none@none.com (Shahid Karim)
content:
IN recent times, a national dialogue has suddenly taken centre stage on the setting up of new provinces/ administrative units. It is perhaps irrelevant to seek its origin. Suffice it to say that the issue has assumed importance politically and is at the heart of all political debate that takes place. In all inquiries, the first step is to ask the right question. The right question that begs an answer is: does our Constitution envisage the creation of new provinces so as to change Pakistan’s geographic contours?
Pakistan is a federal republic and its territories comprise the provinces of Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab and Sindh, apart from the federal capital. Part XI of the Constitution deals with amendment of the Constitution wherein resides a specific provision that relates to an amendment which would have the effect of altering the limits of a province. Clause (4) of Article 239 provides that: “A bill to amend the Constitution which would have the effect of altering the limits of a province shall not be presented to the president for assent unless it has been passed by the provincial assembly of that province by the votes of not less than two-thirds of its total membership.”
At first blush, this clause brings forth the intention of the framers of the Constitution that they plainly understood that Pakistan’s ultimate geographic shape would depend on future laws and constitutional amendments. While emphatically rejecting future unilateral cessation they all accepted the possibility of genuine national legal actions that might redraw the legal map.
It could be redrawn by resort to Article 239 (4) by altering limits of a province or as provided in Article 1 (2)(d)(3) by admitting into the federation new states or areas by law. It is clear that an amendment to alter the limits of a province requires an additional guardrail. It must be passed by the assembly of that province. But such an amendment merely operates to alter the limits of that very province and no more. It does not create a new province thereby. For that, amendment will have to be made in Article 1 which defines the territories of Pakistan and mentions the four provinces at present.
Democracy works if the people are consulted.
Interestingly, limits of a province have not been mentioned in the Constitution. This is delineated in a law enacted as Province of West Pakistan (Dissolution) Order 1970 (P.O No.1 of 1970) which was saved as an existing law at the promulgation of the 1973 Constitution. It can be argued that a mere amendment in Order 1970 should suffice to create a new province but that argument runs a choppy course. The more nuanced question is regarding the legitimacy of the present government to undertake such a structural change in the Constitution.
In representative democracy, this requires a mandate built on the election manifesto upon which a political party is elected to office. There is no cavil that no such mandate was handed to the present government at the last elections since the question was not before them to be considered. That would be a travesty of the essence of representative democracy as enshrined in the Preamble to the Constitution while proclaiming that “we the people of Pakistan … do hereby, through our representatives in the National Assembly, adopt, enact and give to ourselves, this Constitution”. Thus, the Constitution was given to themselves by the people and any change in the basic structure of the Constitution would require essentially a fresh mandate from the people. This, in my opinion, is a constitutional imperative which must be preserved inviolate.
As Nobel laureate Daron Acemoglu said: we did these policies without asking the people, without building a consensus around it and so it became a symbol of elites working against working class communities. Democracy works if you actually ask people. Democracy is about voice and self-government. The failure was we did not create the right type of information ecosystem so that people understood what was the trade-off.
It is very important that we make the commitment that we do not, as the more educated segment of society, impose our values without asking and consulting people. It is an affront to them. There are two ways to seek people’s opinion if the Constitution is to be wrenched out of its original bearings and repurposed. Fresh elections with new provinces as the main plank, or referendum under Article 48(6) of the Constitution. The latter course is piled high with difficulty but the bottom line is that any change of this magnitude requires people’s will and clear mandate. It should not be achieved by deft manoeuvres. 
The writer is a former judge of the Lahore High Court.
Published in Dawn, September 21st, 2026

title: Bridging the gap
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE Global Gender Gap Report 2026 endorses how the dice are loaded against Pakistan’s women. The aggregate performance picture is dark: it is close to the bottom at 143 out of 145 economies, just above Chad and Iran. The gender parity mark rose from last year’s 56.7pc to 59.5pc, shrinking the divide by 5.2pc. The three-notch ascent, billed as the strongest year-on-year progress in a decade, is due to the 91.7pc climb in education parity. Pakistan’s total literacy rate is one of the worst in the world. Piecemeal interventions, and patriarchal systems that chip away at women’s agency have contributed to the downward performance graph in most indices. Some of the highest maternal mortality rates, and regulated access to reproductive health, puts us at 127 in the health and survival category. In a deeply gendered economic and political landscape, Pakistan stands at 144 in female economic participation and opportunity, and 107 in political empowerment, reflecting the dishonesty of political claims. Equal rights elude women in financial services, land and non-land assets, and even justice. Meanwhile, in Sindh’s first Gender Parity Report, women’s abysmal numbers in education and their employment rates in state institutions, including the justice sector, are deeply concerning.
The onus of a skewed scorecard in the primary gauges that drive productivity and progress falls on the government’s failure to install protective ecosystems, counter chauvinistic narratives and respect women’s presence in power structures. Each marker is a mainstay of empowerment. We cannot afford economic strategies where women’s safety, education, employment, and political contributions are not central. These barriers aggravate each other. For instance, education without opportunity makes human capital wither. This, together with a broken and biased criminal justice system, has created an unsafe setting where sexual abuse and other violence are daily realities. To achieve gender equality, justice in these indicators is vital. Female voices cannot remain absent from positions of power. At the same time, progress in silos is insufficient to offset the trenchant systemic constraints that defeat gender parity. Reforms, enforcement of relevant statutes, sensitised law enforcement and legislation will ensure that women are not reduced to an afterthought.

Effective progress necessitates comprehensive reforms, robust enforcement of laws, sensitisation of law enforcement, and meaningful inclusion of women in power structures, as siloed interventions are insufficient.

title: Legal pathways
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
A DROP of 64pc in irregular migration from Pakistan towards Europe is an encouraging development. According to Frontex data cited by the FIA, the decline was recorded in January-February this year compared with the corresponding period in 2025. Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi has now set the considerably more ambitious target of eliminating illegal migration altogether. But the more important question is what Pakistan should expect in return for helping Europe meet one of its central migration goals. If Islamabad is demonstrating that it can curb irregular departures, cooperation with European states should no longer be confined mainly to border controls, interceptions and returns. It should increasingly produce something Pakistan has repeatedly sought: more regulated avenues for its citizens to work abroad. Migration cooperation cannot remain a one-way arrangement.
The framework is already there. The EU-Pakistan Talent Partnership is intended to facilitate labour mobility while matching Pakistani skills with shortages in sectors such as IT, construction, renewable energy, hospitality, agriculture and textiles. Italy has separately allocated 10,500 jobs to Pakistani workers over three years across seasonal and non-seasonal categories. These initiatives are useful, but they should be the beginning rather than the extent of a broader shift. Pakistan’s success in curbing irregular migration gives it stronger grounds to press for wider legal employment opportunities. That would serve both sides. European economies need workers in a range of sectors, while Pakistan has a large population seeking employment abroad. More importantly, legal routes provide an alternative to the smugglers whose business depends on the absence of accessible ones. The next phase of migration cooperation should therefore be judged not only by how sharply irregular departures fall, but by whether safer and lawful routes expand alongside them. If Pakistan is expected to help close the illegal door, Europe should help open the legal one.

topic: Pakistan-Europe Relations, Migration Policy, Labour Mobility

title: Celebrating victory
author: none@none.com (Shaukat Javed)
content:
PAKISTAN has lived with conflict for much of its existence. Its security concerns are real, and its armed forces have repeatedly demonstrated courage. Yet conflict also teaches one that enduring security depends not only on responding to challenges, but on creating conditions in which they do not arise again.
This is worth keeping in mind as Pakistan develops new traditions of commemorating military achievements. On May 10 this year, the country observed the first anniversary of Marka-i-Haq, commemorating Operation Bunyanum Marsoos. The government has announced that May 10 will be observed annually as Marka-i-Haq Day. The anniversary was marked by official ceremonies and patriotic events. Transforming a short, dangerous military confrontation into an annual celebration may not necessarily serve Pakistan’s long-term interests.
In nuclearised South Asia, perhaps victory is best accompanied by humility. Any confrontation that ends without a decisive settlement reminds us how quickly events can move towards escalation. Preparedness is most valuable when accompanied by reflection, restraint and diplomacy. The purpose of national strength remains the preservation of peace.
Pakistan already has another strategic commemoration Youm-i-Takbeer that is observed on May 28 to mark the 1998 nuclear tests. The nuclear deterrent was of historic significance and altered Pakistan’s security calculus. Yet nuclear capability primarily serves deterrence, ensuring that nuclear weapons never have to be used. A nuclear state needs restraint, sound command and control and crisis management.
Perhaps observances could be brought together.
Then comes Defence Day on Sept 6, when the nation remembers the sacrifices of the 1965 war. Perhaps all these observances could be brought together, honouring sacrifices and victories on this single solemn occasion while remembering the human cost of conflict and the importance of peace.
This perspective also lends significance to the inauguration of Yadgar-i-Fatah in Islamabad on the eve of Independence Day. Memorials to fallen soldiers are a natural way for nations to remember sacrifice. But national symbols also acquire meaning from the occasions on which they are presented to the public. Independence Day provides an opportunity to look beyond the events that shaped our statehood and ask how successfully we have fulfilled its larger promise.
Our independence was born in great human suffering. Millions were displaced and hundreds of thousands lost their lives. Since then, Pakistan has experienced wars, political upheavals, economic crises, terrorism and institutional difficulties. Considerable ground remains to be covered. Aug 14 can therefore be more than a patriotic celebration. It can invite an assessment of national performance. What progress have we made in education, health, justice, governance and human development? Why do so many young Pakistanis continue to look overseas for opportunities? Such questions are not a departure from patriotism, they are expressions of it.
Security has several dimensions. Military preparedness remains essential, but sustainable national security also depends on economic strength, political stability, institutional resilience and diplomatic space. Pakistan faces debt, unemployment, inadequate public services and limited fiscal space. Defence is a national priority, but resources are finite and every expenditure carries an opportunity cost.
A confident nation can celebrate its soldiers while recognising its scientists, teachers, entrepreneurs, athletes, artists, doctors and civil servants. National pride can come not only from defending territory, but also from educating children, providing justice and building institutions.
The recent Shan­ghai Cooperation Organisation summit in Bishkek offe­red a reminder of the re­­gional env­ir­onm­ent. Pakistan and India were represented by their pr­­i­me ministers, but the encounter produced little visible thaw. Yet the SCO rem­ains a forum for engagement on counterterrorism, trade and economic cooperation. Pa­­kistan’s assumption of the SCO chair of­fers an opportunity to demonstrate that defending national interests and seeking regional stability need not be competing objectives.
Pakistan should honour its martyrs, remember military successes, maintain effective defence and preserve a credible deterrent. At the same time, the larger national aspiration must remain a Pakistan that is economically strong, politically stable, institutionally mature and diplomatically confident. We need neither forget our victories nor become defined by them. A nation can honour its soldiers without glorifying war, remember sacrifice without perpetuating confrontation, and maintain deterrence while pursuing the peace and prosperity that give national strength its deepest meaning.
The writer is a former IGP Punjab and a former Punjab caretaker home minister.
Published in Dawn, September 20th, 2026

title: AI safety paradox
author: none@none.com (Asad Baig)
content:
ANTHROPIC chief Dario Amodei wants the companies building the world’s most powerful artificial intelligence to slow down. Not stop, but slow the advance of frontier capabilities enough for safety and security work to catch up. He calls it “pacing the frontier”. Amodei says two things have changed. AI is beginning to help build the next generation of AI, raising the possibility of recursive self-improvement. At the same time, frontier agents have started doing things during testing that their developers did not expect or authorise.
Then came Jacob Coxon. The Anthropic resear­cher, who had previously worked at OpenAI, resigned before his equity vested and accused the industry of “gambling with our lives”. His fear that increasingly autonomous systems could threaten humanity before the end of the decade is not a scientific forecast. What makes Coxon important is where the warning comes from, ie, someone who worked inside two laboratories closest to the frontier.
There is, however, an uncomfortable irony in Big Tech sounding the alarm.
Anthropic is not standing outside this economy warning everyone else about it. In 2025, it accepted a two-year Pentagon agreement with a $200 million ceiling to develop AI capabilities for US national security. It built Claude Gov for classified environments and says its systems support intelligence analysis, operational planning, and cyber operations. Anthropic says it later refused demands that would have removed its restrictions around mass domestic surveillance and fully autonomous weapons. The contradiction is that companies warning that powerful AI may become difficult to control are simultaneously moving it deeper into military and intelligence systems.
AI regulators should operate transparently and remain subject to judicial oversight.
The contradiction goes beyond Anthropic. An Associated Press investigation found commercial Microsoft and OpenAI technology being used by the Israeli military in Gaza and Lebanon, including in intelligence systems connected to targeting. Microsoft later said its review found no evidence that its technology had been used to harm civilians. AI is already being folded into warfare while the debate about what these systems may become is still taking shape.
Anthropic’s own threat reporting makes the concern more concrete. The company says it has disrupted attempts to use Claude for cyber operations, surveillance, conventional weapons development, and biological misuse.
The more revealing incidents came during safety testing. In July, OpenAI disclosed that models in cyber evaluations circumvented isolation controls, reached the internet, and compromised parts of OpenAI’s own research infrastructure and systems belonging to Hugging Face. Anthropic initially disclosed three cases in which Claude models gained unauthorised access to real third-party systems during evaluations and later identified a fourth.
None of this means an AI has suddenly become conscious or malicious. The immediate problem is scale. A capable hacker, weapons engineer or surveillance operation needs expertise, time and people. AI can lower those barriers, work at machine speed, and let one operator run several specialised agents at once. Capabilities once concentrated in governments or specialist organisations could become cheaper and easier to reproduce. Amodei’s answer is to give independent evaluators permanent, employee-like access to frontier laboratories and their safety processes. He also wants companies to coordinate around common standards and eventually some form of international agreement.
Questions, however, remain as to who chooses the evaluators. Who pays? What can they publish? And what happens if an evaluator says a model is unsafe and the company releases it anyway?
Amodei points to organisations such as METR, an independent nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI systems for dangerous capabilities and loss of control risks. METR says it takes no funding from frontier AI companies or donations directed by their employees, although those companies provide substantial free access to models. But an evaluator can test and warn. Unless someone can act on those findings, the final decision remains with the company.
Meta offers a useful precedent. Its Oversight Board was designed to operate at arm’s length, and its decisions on individual content cases bind Meta. Its wider policy recommendations do not. In 2025, the board criticised Meta for making major moderation changes without publicly demonstrating adequate human rights due diligence. However, it lacked enforcement power. The bottom line is, independent oversight is great. It can improve accountability but will not necessarily shift ultimate power.
Thus, my argument isn’t against self-regulation. AI is moving too quickly for governments to understand every capability before it appears, and companies can impose safeguards faster than legislatures can pass laws. But voluntary restraint cannot be the final layer of accountability.
Politics makes even that difficult. Donald Trump has made American AI leadership part of his competition with China and has dismissed the latest safety alarm, arguing that slowing development would benefit Beijing. Whether China is actually better placed to win that competition is a larger question, and one I am leaving for another piece. The point here is simpler: commercial competition and geopolitics reward speed at precisely the moment some of the people building these systems are asking for caution.
Regulation is necessary, but it carries its own dangers. Rules written largely by AI companies could entrench the biggest firms. Rules written too broadly by governments could turn ‘AI safety’ into an excuse for censorship, surveillance or control over legitimate research and speech.
A better approach would be risk-based. Low-risk applications need little intervention, while systems crossing defined thresholds in areas such as cyber capability, biological risk, weapons, critical infrastructure or autonomous action should face much tougher requirements. Frontier models could undergo mandatory independent testing before deployment, serious incidents should be disclosed, and companies should retain liability for foreseeable harms.
Evaluators need protected funding, and whistleblowers need legal safeguards. Regulators should operate transparently and remain subject to judicial oversight. Most importantly, the rules should target dangerous capabilities and conduct, not political viewpoints or lawful expression.
The difficult question is no longer whether AI needs oversight. Even some of the people building the most powerful systems now say it does. The challenge is designing rules strong enough to matter without giving either corporations or governments powers that create a different kind of danger. 
The writer is the founder of Media Matters for Democracy.

title: Kohat attack
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
FRIDAY’S attack in Kohat marks a further escalation by Pakistan’s enemies. They targeted a mosque in Kohat’s old Police Lines with an explosives-laden vehicle, then attempted to storm the compound and attack police facilities in the ensuing chaos.
At least 23, including 17 police personnel and officials, were martyred in this dastardly assault on worshippers. More than 100 were wounded. But police and security forces regrouped quickly and launched a valiant counterassault, eliminating all but two of the attackers within hours of the initial bombing. The remaining two were neutralised in a clean-up operation that extended overnight, supervised by some of the top police and counterterrorism officials, with one holed-up terrorist killed and the other blowing themselves up rather than face the consequences of their actions.
    
The operation produced considerable acts of courage, not least by the additional inspector-general of the CTD, who was injured by a grenade yet returned to conclude the clean-up.
The nation will mourn the lives lost and pray for those who were injured. The nation will also demand swift justice for those who lost loved ones.
The group which claimed the attack has, by attacking worshippers on what Muslims consider the holiest occasion of the week, not only shown that it observes no ethical limits, but also that it is operating with a single goal: to cause maximum bloodshed and harm.
The Ittehadul Mujahideen, an umbrella organisation of terrorist outfits, is, according to the Jamestown Foundation think tank, believed to operate from safe havens across the border, share intelligence and coordinate attacks with its terrorist factions, and run organised digital campaigns. It has apparently used drone technologies to deadly effect while targeting security forces and installations in the past. As such, it is considered in some circles to be a more serious and sophisticated threat than the TTP. It needs to be treated as such.
    
The KP police must be better equipped and trained. They are facing an enemy which is increasingly using modern technology to cause bloodshed. They must be supported with the equipment, strategies and technologies they need to effectively limit and counter the constant, deadly threat they face.
Simultaneously, the authorities need to review the approaches being taken to counter violent actors. National policy on counterterrorism requires recalibration and revisiting, especially regarding its diplomatic, political and social aspects, which must be addressed together to secure stable dividends.
Sadly, the public’s attention is so fixated on social, political and economic problems that the terrorism crisis has been pushed to the margins of national discourse. Pakistan must confront these networks with the full force of the state and the law, but cannot do so effectively till its own house is in order.

title: Dangers of a wider war
author: none@none.com (Maleeha Lodhi)
content:
A DANGEROUS new front has opened in the Middle East war. Yemen and the Red Sea are now the latest battleground. This has widened the regional conflict and added another layer to the escalating confrontation between the US and Iran. The entry of new actors, Iran-aligned Ansarullah Houthis and Iraqi militias, poses a serious security and economic threat to Saudi Arabia. Oil prices have soared as a result and fuel supplies to global markets have become more uncertain. Diplomacy is deadlocked. Efforts to revive talks between the US and Iran had stalled before these developments. Now they appear to have hit a wall.
The dramatic turn of events came with the Houthis’ lightning military offensive along Yemen’s west coast, which culminated in their capture of the strategic Red Sea port city of Mocha and Perim island in the Bab al-Mandeb strait. This gave them control of a key shipping route. Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces failed to prevent the advance and the loss of more strategic territory to the Houthis. At the same time, the Houthis launched attacks on Saudi energy infrastructure. The vital East-West pipeline across Saudi Arabia was forced to close after a drone strike by Iraq-based militias. Iran’s closure of the Strait of Hormuz and Houthi control of another maritime chokepoint — the narrow Bab al-Mandeb strait — has severely constrained KSA’s ability to export oil.
Tehran claims the Houthis are acting independently. Nevertheless, the action by the Houthis and Iraqi militias could have been coordinated by Iran to mount pressure on the US and counter its attempt to loosen Iranian control of the Strait of Hormuz by American warships escorting more vessels through the waterway. It may also be a res­ponse to US economic warfare which is placing fur­ther strain on the Iranian economy. Multiple Saudi air strikes on the Houthis have failed to dislodge them from the territory they have seized across Yemen. The militia continues to control the entire western coast of the country along the Red Sea.
The fighting marks the re-eruption of a conflict that began in 2014 in Yemen’s civil war between a Saudi-led coalition spearheaded by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman and the Houthis. This came to a halt with a ceasefire in 2022. But the truce broke down this July when the Houthis announced a blockade of Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea ports following an attack on Sanaa airport by Saudi-backed forces.   
Beyond the economic fallout the political implications of a spreading conflict are also serious.
The deteriorating situation confronts MBS with a dilemma: to escalate or pursue a diplomatic path. His efforts to secure US military intervention have not succeeded so far although there are unconfirmed reports that the US is weighing options to launch military strikes against the Houthis. He spoke twice to President Donald Trump asking for direct US help but Washington has been reluctant to join the fight. Trump’s comments during a visit to Ireland are revealing. “The Houthis called us and they don’t want to fight with us,” he said. “They don’t want us to go after them and would much prefer not having us involved, and they’re letting most ships go through. It’s just one country they’re not too happy with. And we’ll get that straightened out.”
The remarks indicate Trump’s unwillingness to intervene even as his most important Gulf ally comes under fierce attack.Washington clearly doesn’t want to shift focus from the conflict with Iran, where it is bogged down, having failed to gain the upper hand and compel Iran to submit to its demands. The US military is already overstretched and facing a serious munition shortfall after nearly seven months of war. These problems will worsen if the US intervenes in the Saudi-Houthis conflict. The US Central Comm­and estimates the Iran war has cost over $43 billion.
Meanwhile, speculation that Riyadh may invoke the Makkah joint defence agreement with Pakistan and Turkiye has so far come to nothing. Pakistan has given no indication of going beyond verbal support to the kingdom and condemnation of Houthi actions even though it has troops and fighter jets deployed there. As the Foreign Office spokesman put it, the pact is defensive in nature and no military plan is under discussion. Prince Mohammed has however held talks with the Centcom chief amid reports that the US is helping KSA with targeting and intelligence. 
For all the assessments by many Western analysts that Iran’s regional allies have been weakened by the war with the US, the latest events show this is not the case. The ‘axis of resistance’ is not only intact but potent enough to launch a two-pronged assault on KSA plunging it into a crisis. Meanwhile, Iran’s leverage has increased because in addition to its grip over the Strait of Hormuz its ally, the Houthi militia, now controls the Red Sea energy chokepoint, Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which can be seen as a strategic gain for Tehran.  
The economic impact of an escalating wider conflict can be far-reaching. Already the oil price has soared to above $100 a barrel. Gas prices too have risen. Uncertainty about global energy supplies, which are already running low, may drive prices even higher. This despite the Houthi leadership’s assurance that it will not block all commercial shipping in the Red Sea, only Saudi-linked ships. With its oil production having fallen, the world’s largest oil exporter, Saudi Arabia, has already cut crude oil shipments. The damage to its 1,200-kilometre export pipeline threatens the loss of four per cent of global oil supply. In the US, the oil price rise has contributed to pushing US borrowing costs to their highest level since 2007. The bond market is being adversely affected by fears over energy prices and inflation. 
Beyond the economic fallout for countries across the world, the political implications of a spreading conflict are no less serious. With new actors having entered the fray — and more might be sucked in — diplomacy will face new challenges in forging agreements among so many players. This will make the diplomatic process more complex and difficult even if there is willingness among the warring parties to find a negotiated end to the conflict. Unfortunately, a regional meeting in Oman between Iran and Gulf states to discuss control of the Strait of Hormuz and work out an interim arrangement has been postponed. For now, neither the US nor Iran are prepared to budge from their position and resume negotiations. In the end, the outcome may hinge on who can endure economic pain the longest. 
The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
Published in Dawn, September 21st, 2026

title: An eye on Balochistan border
author: none@none.com (Muhammad Amir Rana)
content:
THE intensifying Yemeni Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia have triggered a debate over the possible activation of the Makkah accord. Statements and clarifications about possible and emerging scenarios are coming from all stakeholders.
But a recent incident in Saravan county in Sistan-Baluchestan, close to the Pakistan border, has also drawn attention to the Iran-Pakistan border region. This has broadened the debate over the Gulf region’s security and evolving geopolitics, and Pakistan’s role in it.
The incident was reported on Sept 12, when heavy fighting between Iranian security forces and unidentified gunmen spread across parts of Saravan, with reports of attacks on military vehicles and dozens of security personnel killed or wounded. Although the identity of the armed group is not yet clear, some analysts have attributed the attack to Jaish al-Adl or the People’s Fighters Front, an alliance of several groups, reportedly including Jaish al-Adl.
Since the start of the conflict in West Asia, Balochistan’s security dynamics have changed. The conflict has altered the operating environment in which an existing insurgency was already functioning.
    
The BLA and other allied groups have intensified their terrorist activities. The economic blockade announced by these groups has disrupted transportation and halted economic activity, particularly in the mineral sector. The closure of the frontier with Afghanistan and the partial closure of the border with Iran have contributed to the crisis. Taken together, these developments have affected the region’s security, internal political dynamics and geopolitical environment, bringing new risks to the province.
An angle that has largely been overlooked in the broader conflict theatre in this area is the state of affairs along the Pakistan-Iran border, which stretches for around 900 kilometres and where multiple violent religious and nationalist insurgent groups, as well as transnational criminal networks, operate. The border’s porous nature raises further security concerns. According to media reports, Pakistani security institutions had placed Balochistan on high alert because of the possible fallout from the Iran war.
The situation along the Pakistan-Iran border in the broader conflict has been largely overlooked.
The Jan 16, 2024, Iranian strike inside Pakistan, allegedly targeting Jaish al-Adl hideouts, followed by Pakistan’s retaliatory strikes on militant targets in Iran, changed the dynamics of their bilateral relations and prompted greater security cooperation. That cooperation has largely remained intact.
However, the recent Saravan attack has raised questions about how the changing regional environment could affect the future course of frontier security, particularly as Pakistan’s border with Afghanistan remains closed and Iran is an alternative, although very expensive, route for transnational trade.
For Iran, if the Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) has to concentrate its resources on US and Israeli strikes, the Strait of Hormuz and operations in the Gulf, Sistan-Baluchestan could become a per­ipheral theatre competing for Iranian security resources. Any escalation of tensions betw­een Iran and Pakistan is in neither country’s interest. However, non-state actors always try to find an opportunity in evolving conflicts, especially when wider regional contexts provide them with more meaning and relevance in the conflict theatre.
The BLA and other insurgent groups appear to have viewed the war as an opportunity to escalate their operations, perhaps hoping that they could eventually be considered as potential proxies against Iran, as happened in Syria with America’s partnership with the Syrian Demo­cratic Forces. The SDF was a coalition that included Kurdish armed groups such as the YPG and YPJ, along with Syrian Arab and Assyrian/ Christian elements.
The BLA has also issued a few statements supporting US strikes on Iran. Perhaps the BLA believes it can find meaning in the wider conflict in West Asia. Still, the BLA is missing a point in its calculation: the convergence of US, Pakistani, and Saudi geopolitical and strategic interests will persist in the coming years.
At the same time, Jaish al-Adl and several smaller groups have reportedly sought to broaden their activities against the Quds Force and IRGC. The group remained relatively quiet until Iranian security forces launched an operation against suspected terrorists in Saravan last August, reportedly apprehending several Jaish al-Adl members and killing one. During the operation, security forces said they recovered a significant arsenal of military hardware, including dozens of Kalash­nikov automatic rifles, hand grenades, RPG-7 launchers, around 20 kilograms of C-4 military-grade explosives, 150 rounds of ammunition, and several Starlink satellite internet devices.
The Saravan operation reported last week has since been interpreted in multiple ways, mostly based on assumptions rather than established evidence. One popular theory links the attack to the intensification of Houthi strikes on Saudi Arabia.
    
The incident also occurred while Pakistan was diplomatically engaged with Iran. According to a media report, subsequently denied by Pakistan, Islamabad had conveyed a Saudi message to Tehran asking Iran to restrain the Houthis.
A popular perception in the border region of Balochistan is that if Iran can use the Houthis as a proxy against Saudi Arabia, it must also expect the possibility of a similar reaction from Saudi Arabia. The Sunni militias operating in Sistan-Baluchestan, from Jundullah to the People’s Fighters Front, are said to be proxies of foreign powers including the US and Saudi Arabia. That perception is nurturing new theories. A few of them are critical of Pakistan too.
Whether such perceptions translate into an actual Saudi strategy is another question. But perceptions themselves can influence the behaviour of armed groups and local actors, particularly in a region where terrorist networks, cross-border tribal connections and informal economic networks overlap.
Beyond all the theories surrounding the strategic calculus of West Asia and the prospects of Saudi proxies emerging along the Pakistan-Iran border, one fact remains clear: Pakistan cannot afford further chaos in the border region of Balochistan. Any expansion of the regional conflict in an already fragile security environment could make the country’s internal security dynamics considerably more complex.
The writer is a security analyst.
Published in Dawn, September 20th, 2026

title: Strategic stability
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
IN a world awash with violence, where the old geopolitical rules of the game are being rapidly rewritten, there is a need for states to display maturity and rational behaviour in statecraft. This is all the more true in troubled regions such as South Asia, which have been witnessing friction for decades, and where nuclear weapons are part of the equation. Addressing a workshop in Islamabad recently, adviser to the National Command Authority and former head of the Strategic Plans Division retired Lt-Gen Mazhar Jamil highlighted the shrinking space for diplomacy in South Asia. He added that the erosion of arms control frameworks and reliance on hard power were creating “new challenges to strategic stability in South Asia”. While criticising India’s “military adventurism and hegemonic approaches”, the official made a crucial observation: there was no space for war between two nuclear states.
This should be clear to any level-headed individual. However, high-level officials in the Indian military, as well as the political elite, have — particularly since last year’s hostilities — been making increasingly jingoistic statements directed at Pakistan. In May, the Indian army chief — who has since retired — hurled unacceptable threats at this country, which were described by ISPR as “hubristic”. Indian political leaders have been making similarly unhinged comments. While such language may attract a few votes and please extremist lobbies within India, it does lasting damage to the cause of peace in South Asia, especially at a time when both nations have only recently emerged from a dangerous encounter that could have spiralled into all-out war. 
War in a nuclear neighbourhood is not an option. Pakistani officials have reiterated this, and there is a need for similar rational behaviour from responsible military and civilian actors in India. There is huge bilateral mistrust at the moment. Yet to prevent a catastrophe in the subcontinent, both sides, particularly India, need to restart the dialogue process. This can begin with small steps, such as regular contact between military officials from both sides to ensure misunderstandings do not escalate into something larger. In parallel, diplomatic contacts and Track II efforts need to be resumed. While it is difficult to foresee peace in the immediate future, such steps can at least help in conflict management, while ensuring that the channels of communication are kept open. But perhaps the biggest need is for Indian officials to stop their inflammatory rhetoric against Pakistan, which is even more irresponsible at a time when the flames of war are burning not too far from South Asia. Hopefully, restraint and sustained dialogue can lead to bilateral trust and peace between Pakistan and India.

title: Final frontiers
author: none@none.com (Zarrar Khuhro)
content:
IN his first term in office, US President Donald Trump announced the creation of the Space Force, a new branch of the US military to add to the existing army, navy, air force, etc. Now, in 2026, not only has the US announced for the first time that it has actually put weapons in space, it has also released the uniforms designed for the Space Force. To no one’s surprise, they look identical to the uniforms of the Imperial Navy in Star Wars. In case you’ve been exiled to Alpha Centauri for the last century, those were the Bad Guys.
Unfortunate Sith parallels aside, the US has not revealed the exact nature of the weaponry but US military leaders have previously spoken about the need for space-based military capabilities, purportedly to counter alleged Russian and Chinese capabilities. In particular, the US has been looking at anti-satellite systems designed to disable or blind an adversary’s eye-in-the-sky capabilities.
That capability has been quite irksome for the US during its disastrous war on Iran, with reports claiming that Chinese and Russian satellites provided information for Iranian drone and missile strikes, enabling pinpoint accuracy when it comes to targeting US assets in the region. And then, a few weeks ago, an orbiting Chinese satellite — Yaogan-50 — disintegrated into over 40 pieces. Was this a coincidence or a demonstration of America’s now-declared capabilities? We’ll likely never know.
Development of space-based weapons continues.
What we do know is that China — which has protested against the US announcement — has tried to develop anti-satellite capabilities of its own likely based on the philosophy that while space-based weapons are difficult to deploy and expensive, countermeasures against enemy satellites may be an easier way out, similar to the philosophy of area denial by fielding anti-ship and aircraft carrier missiles.
In 2007, China successfully targeted an aging weather satellite with a ground-based missile. Next year, the US followed suit by shooting down a military satellite it claimed was about to crash, and in 2010, China shot down another satellite. But since destroying satellites entirely can be messy, capabilities are being developed to ‘blind’ them instead, rendering them useless; along with the US, Russia and China are also developing and deploying ground-based directed-energy weapons and satellite-blinding lasers. The US is already deploying the Meadowlands Counter Communication System which can fry orbital satellites using electromagnetic beams.
In one sense, the first shot in the Space Wars was fired in World War II when German scientists created the V1 and V2 rocket and missile, the predecessors of the cruise and ballistic missiles, but the real push to weaponise space began with the space race where the USSR scored early wins with the launch of Sputnik in 1957 and by making cosmonaut Yuri Gagarin the first man in space four years later.
In 1962, the US conducted a high-altitude nuclear weapons test codenamed Starfish Prime — not just as a warning to the USSR but also to see if the resulting electromagnetic pulse would disrupt nearby satellites. With the spectre of nuclear weapons in space looming large and talk of potential military bases on the moon, the Outer Space Treaty was signed in 1967, prohibiting the placement of nuclear weapons or other WMDs and proclaiming that no country would seek sovereignty over the moon.
But the development of space-based weapons continued nevertheless. In 1974, the Soviets successfully tested the first known armed satellite. The Salyut-3 satellite was equ­ip­ped with an air­craft cannon from which it fi­­­red a single rou­nd proving that it was ind­eed possible to arm satellites alth­o­ugh quest­ions of accura­cy and feasibility rem­­­­­ained.
Over a decade later, the USSR returned to the concept by testing a heavy satellite — the Polyus — which was armed with a carbon-dioxide laser and a cannon to boot. However, it failed to launch.
Then there was Reagan and his ‘Star Wars’ initiative that envisioned a national ballistic missile shield for the US, some components of which would be space-based: the ‘Brilliant Pebbles’ project envisioned the deployment of thousands of small interceptors in orbit that would then collide with Soviet ICBMs — a sort of Patriot Missile system in space. Other proposals included satellites armed with lasers. Whether or not Reagan knew, most of these plans were impossible to implement because of cost and lack of requisite technology. But the USSR took it seriously enough to try and play catch-up. Arguably, the costs thus incurred played a part in the downfall of the Soviet Empire.
But this isn’t the Cold War anymore, and the rapid technological developments we are seeing now mean that ideas once safely relegated to the realm of science fiction are becoming fact. Watch the skies.
The writer is a journalist.

title: Restrained court
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
THE state continues to leave no stone unturned in demonstrating that there is no rule of law in Pakistan. Even the highest courts appear to have no writ where the will of the state is concerned.
This week, for yet another time, a Supreme Court order expired at the gates of a prison. The administration overruled the Supreme Court’s bail orders for Imaan Mazari-Hazir and Hadi Ali Chattha late Thursday evening with a hitherto unknown FIR, reportedly carrying a terrorism charge inked in by hand.
    
The young couple are well-regarded in legal and rights circles. They were known for taking up cases few others would be willing to touch. That, precisely, is what seems to have irked some in the corridors of power, which led to the two being sentenced last January to 17 years in prison for posting ‘harmful’ content on social media.
They have remained in custody since then.
When the Supreme Court ordered their release on bail, the state swung into action. It discovered a case registered 18 months ago that had never been pursued or consolidated, and activated it hours before they were meant to be released. An Anti-Terrorism Court promptly remanded them to judicial custody.
The sequence of events leaves many questions unanswered. If such a serious terrorism case had been pending against the two lawyers, why was it not pursued for such a long period? And why was it not brought before the Supreme Court’s attention when the decision to allow bail was being made?
Furthermore, the new case pertains mainly to Pakistan Penal Code violations, and it seems the two were only brought before an ATC judge due to a terrorism charge added as an afterthought. The ATCs, which were created to prosecute violent terrorists, seem to have become a general-purpose tool for handling inconvenient people.
    
The rulers of the day should remember that precedents are being set. If every bail order can be neutralised with a dormant FIR, this tool will invariably be used against any citizen who falls afoul of the state.
The Supreme Court must also decide how far it is willing to allow itself to be subjected to external pressure. If the executive can do with a court order whatever it pleases without any consequence whatsoever, it also exposes the judiciary’s own unwillingness to enforce its writ.
Published in Dawn, September 19th, 2026

title: Urban air pollution
author: none@none.com (Umair Ahmad Ghumman)
content:
ACCORDING to IQAir’s World Air Quality Report 2025, Pakistan recorded the worst air quality among 143 monitored countries, with an annual average PM2.5 concentration more than 13 times the WHO guideline. The Pakistan Economic Survey 2025-26 confirms that around 22,000 deaths each year are linked to air pollution. Four of the world’s 10 most polluted cities are in Pakistan. Lahore is the worst, followed by Faisalabad, Multan and Peshawar. This insight argues that Pakistan’s urban air pollution crisis stems mainly from local factors, with transport being the largest contributor. Long-term improvements will come from consistent, city-specific reforms rather than temporary emergency measures that emerge each smog season.
Pakistan’s National Clean Air Policy, approved by the federal cabinet in 2023, attributes 235,000 premature deaths annually to air pollution exposure. Similarly, the University of Chicago’s Air Quality Life Index suggests that complying with the WHO guideline could extend average life expectancy by 3.3 years, and by more than five in Lahore and Peshawar. Punjab took the serious step of declaring a health emergency. At the same time, provincial records showed nearly 1.93 million respiratory cases in just one month. Unicef warned that 11m children under five breathe toxic air each day.
The Pakistan Air Quality Initiative’s national landscape report from December 2025, which is the country’s first comprehensive inventory that looks at each city individually, helps clear up a lot of the confusion. In Lahore, transport makes up 35 per cent of PM2.5 levels. Rawalpindi-Islamabad sees transport as the main source at 53pc; Peshawar is at 51pc, and Karachi stands out as being predominantly industrial, with 49pc from industry and port operations. Since each city faces different pollution sources, the situation calls for tailored solutions.
Cleaner fuel is most effective when paired with cleaner engines.
With Pakistan’s heavy reliance on roads, transport has emerged as the top urban issue. In Lahore, studies link about 36pc of fine-particle pollution to diesel and two-stroke exhaust, with two- and three-wheelers being particularly high emitters. Peshawar’s problem is compounded by over 50,000 unregistered two-stroke engine rickshaws, a vehicle class that emits more particulate matter per kilometre than any other on the road. After the decline caused by the 2022 floods, sales bounced back in 2024, making Pakistan one of the fastest-growing two-wheeler markets globally. Many cities have faced similar choices between making long-term structural changes and applying temporary solutions.
Peshawar’s TransPeshawar bus rapid transit system, which uses hybrid-electric buses, moves over 345,000 passengers daily, making it the busiest BRT in the country. Lahore’s Metrobus and Orange Line together transport more than 250,000 people each day. The Rawalpindi-Islamabad Metrobus system serves around 135,000 commuters daily, now supported by 160 electric buses imported from China. Expanding and linking these systems is a powerful step, offering the greatest benefits.
Cleaner fuel is most effective when paired with cleaner engines. Pakistan is now providing Euro-5 fuel nationwide and aims to reach Euro-6 standards by 2030. However, the impact is limited because there is no strict enforcement of vehicle-emission standards; for example, Punjab has only 32 inspection stations to serve over 24m vehicles. Implementing mandatory emission testing and fitness certification could be a simple yet significant step forward.
Improving rail freight and the ML-1 corridor can help red­uce heavy diesel trucking on urban roads, which in turn can help lower city pollution. That’s a great reason to support the Rail­w­ays’ goal of increasing its passenger modal share from around 4pc to 20pc.
Renewing the fleet is the next positive step. A trustworthy scrappage scheme for the oldest and most polluting vehicles would be an effective follow-up. Electrification then directly tackles the most harmful segment. The National Electric Vehicle Policy 2025-30 aims for 30pc of new vehicle sales to be electric by 2030, supported by over Rs100 billion in incentives. Focusing on two- and three-wheelers offers the fastest path to cleaner city air.
The response should match the problem: a city-specific programme built on mass transit, cleaner fuels and fleet electrification. Paid parking to discourage private vehicle use, organised parking facilities, and a congestion charge in major urban centres would reduce traffic and increase dem­and for mass transit. Development of public transport infrastructure should be prioritised over the construction of new flyovers and underpasses. Clean air is a strategic priority rather than a seasonal concern. 
The writer is an assistant research associate at the Institute for Strategic Studies, Research and Analysis, National Defence University.
Published in Dawn, September 19th, 2026

title: Why isn’t the economy growing?
author: none@none.com (Syed Sardar Ali)
content:
DURING the roughly 150-year period between 1760 and World War I, England, the countries of northwest Europe, and the US went through the economic transformation of the Industrial Revolution. Real per capita GDP, which had remained stagnant at $2-3 per day, started to rise. Real wages that had historically remained slightly above subsistence level doubled. The percentage of labour force employed in agriculture plummeted. The West’s share of global manufacturing — around 25 per cent before the Industrial Revolution — jumped to more than 80pc by 1914. Some economic historians have labelled this shift as humanity’s ‘great escape’ from poverty, disease, and squalor.
In the past 200 years, Japan, South Korea, and China stand as the only non-European nations to have bridged the economic divide with the West. These countries accomplished in decades what the West achieved in centuries by sustaining long periods of nearly double-digit economic growth.
    
After the destruction wreaked by World War II, Japan grew at an average annual rate of nearly 10pc from 1955 to 1973. In 1968, it surpassed Germany to become the second largest economy. Starting in the early 1960s, South Korea entered a period of sustained economic growth, described as the ‘Miracle on the Han River’. Real GDP increased 25-fold in three decades. In 1996, South Korea became a member of the OECD. In the 40 years following the ‘reform and opening up’ of 1978, China’s economy grew at an average annual rate of about 9.5pc, increasing the size of its GDP roughly 35- to 40-fold in real terms. In the process, China lifted nearly 800 million people out of poverty and became the world’s largest economy in PPP terms in 2014.
The high-speed economic growth of the East Asian economies displayed three characteristics. First, the period of rapid economic growth was preceded by fundamental restructuring of society’s political and cultural institutions. Second, the shift from an agricultural to industrial economy was spearheaded by the state. Third, during the transformation period, the attainment of econo­m­­ic goals was prioritised over political freedoms.
For Pakistanis to live better, the economy must grow at near double-digit rates for decades.
From 1945 until 1951, Gen Douglas MacArthur presided over Japan’s post-World War II transformation as supreme commander of the allied powers. He had Emperor Hirohito issue a rescript denouncing his divinity, promulgated a new constitution, carried out land reforms, changed the education system, and introduced American cultural elements to Japanese life. In South Korea, before Gen Park seized power in 1961, land reforms had already been accomplished through the initiative of the United States Army Military Government in Korea. Gen Park launched the New Community Movement, promoted traditional ethno-nationalism, and strictly regulated social life. During the first 30 years after the revolution of 1949, the Communist Party of China dismantled the 2,000-year-old imperial system, gave land title to nearly 300m peasants, and laid the foundations of a modern state.
The post-World War II reconstruction in Japan was led by the ‘iron triangle’ of bureaucrats from the trade and industry ministry, Liberal Democratic Party politicians, and the captains of Japan’s leading industrial conglomerates. In South Korea, Gen Park adopted the policy of export-led economic growth by providing subsidised credit to chaebols, suppressing domestic demand, and quashing labour unions. In China, the state laid the foundations of basic and heavy industry through financial and technical Soviet assistance. Even after Deng Xiaoping’s liberalisation, the state still controls strategic sectors of the economy and takes the lead in pioneering new technologies.
    
Nominally, Japan was a parliamentary democracy during the post-World War II economic tra­n­s­­formation, but the Liberal Democratic Party re­­mained in power for 38 years in what is described as a ‘one-and-a-half party system’. Following a coup in 1961, Gen Park first ruled South Korea as a military dictator and then adopted a constitution giving him near absolute powers without term limits. China has remained a one-party-led state since its founding in 1949. Deng Xiaoping, who launched the economic ‘reform and opening up’ in 1978, rejected dem­ands for Western-style democracy and suppressed the 1989 demonstrations in Tiananmen Square.
In varying degrees, these conditions were present in all countries that successfully transformed into industrialised nations. Pakistan experienced something similar during its first two decades, when it attempted land reforms, passed the Muslim Family Laws Ordinance, and adopted the five-year planning system, with input from the Harvard Advisory Group. All the economic and social gains of these early decades were lost starting in the 1970s. In 1998, Pakistan discontinued the practice of drawing five-year plans and began transitioning to a medium-term development framework. Slow growth in the last two decades has caused Pakistan to fall behind its South Asian neighbours in living standards. The manufacturing sector represents less than 13pc of GDP, and the country runs an average annual trade deficit of around $30 billion.
Harsh policy measures have stabilised Pakistan’s economy. During FY2024-2025, Pakistan recorded a current account surplus because of import restrictions and robust remittances. Fiscal deficit dropped to a multi-decade low of 2.6pc of GDP in 2025-26. Record-high inflation has come down to more manageable levels. Pakistan’s sovereign credit rating has improved because of lower external risks. However, growth has remained stagnant at around 3.5pc per annum for the last decade. The IMF projects an annual growth rate of 3.5pc for 2026-27, which is barely sufficient to offset the depreciation of the capital stock and compensate for population growth.
For Pakistanis to experience any meaningful improvement in living standards, the economy needs to grow at near double-digit rates for several decades. Our current subsistence level agricultural economy with a rudimentary level of industrialisation has reached the limits of its productive capacity. Transformative growth can only come by making the quantum leap to industry. However, industrialisation requires us to fundamentally restructure the political and social order of society, and the state should lead the industrialisation process, with political differences subordinated to the pursuit of economic goals. The poverty trap will not be broken by incremental policy reforms. It requires restructuring the entire system of society.
The writer has a background in public administration. He has worked with international financial institutions, including the World Bank.
Published in Dawn, September 18th, 2026

title: Beyond the dollar
author: none@none.com (Editorial)
content:
PAKISTAN’S plan to seek a larger currency-swap facility with China while pursuing a similar arrangement with the US is a prudent financial diversification effort. Despite improvements, our foreign exchange reserves remain vulnerable to debt repayments, import costs and external shocks. More liquidity backstops can ease that pressure. A currency swap lets central banks temporarily exchange their respective currencies, giving the liquidity-constrained country access to foreign exchange for payments and easing pressure during shortages. Pakistan has drawn China’s 30bn yuan facility, due for renewal in 2027 when Islamabad seeks an increase, while awaiting America’s approval for $10bn.
Pursuing both arrangements would give Pakistan more options when external financing comes under pressure. The Chinese facility can also support trade and payments with China in renminbi, reducing the immediate need for dollars for some transactions. A dollar facility would provide more direct support for dollar-denominated obligations and foreign-exchange market pressures. But the limits of these facilities must be clear. A drawn facility creates a liability that must be repaid. The State Bank reserve figures should therefore disclose and distinguish between freely available reserves and funds with repayment obligations. That said, these facilities are not a substitute for economic reform. They can provide breathing space, but cannot permanently strengthen the external account. The risk would be to use easier access to liquidity to postpone the difficult work of raising productivity, expanding exports and reducing dependence on external borrowing. For now, however, the strategy is useful. Pakistan needs stronger buffers against oil-price spikes, debt-service pressures and other external shocks. A wider network of bilateral liquidity facilities can reduce the risk of a temporary shock turning into another protracted balance-of-payment crisis. The aim should be simple. Build credible external buffers and use them sparingly. More importantly, increase exports, attract stable FDI and boost the economy’s capacity to earn foreign exchange.
Published in Dawn, September 19th, 2026
