title: Showing empathy
author: none@none.com (Huma Yusuf)
content:
ON the 100-day anniversary of the Oct 7, 2023, attack by Hamas against Israel, and after 25,000 Palestinians had been killed by Israel’s retaliatory strikes, then US president Joe Biden made a shocking statement: “I will never forget the grief and the suffering I have heard in my meetings with the families of the American hostages. No one should have to endure even one day of what they have gone through, much less 100.”
His statement did not reference the thousands of slaughtered Palestinians, including women and children, or the intentional targeting of hospitals and journalists. Nor did it acknowledge the International Court of Justice hearings that had begun days prior to investigate allegations of Israeli war crimes. The statement was derided as “shameful” by Barnett Rubin, a US foreign policy expert who knew Biden from their time in the Obama administration.
Biden’s one-sided statement is flagged in a new book, Crossing the Red Line, by award-winning Pakistani journalist Akbar Shahid Ahmed, which documents how the Biden administration enabled Israeli atrocities in Gaza, and set the stage for the widening of the Middle East conflict during the current Trump administration.
In a book filled with examples of US negligence and complicity in breaches of international law in Gaza, this example resonates. Speaking last week at a book launch event, Ahmed used the example to illustrate Biden’s tunnel vision when it came to the Israel-Palestine conflict, specifically his inability to acknowledge the plight of Palestinians. In Biden’s and his administration’s perspective, all Palestinian children killed were the children of Hamas fighters; reports of famine in Gaza were exaggerated; schools and hospitals were Hamas hideouts; and intelligence or humanitarian reports suggesting otherwise were forced to caveat findings or report selectively.
The need for engagement is too often simplified.
The president’s inability to humanise Palestinians or empathise with their predicament was, Ahmed argued, a determinant of the US’s Israel policy and its failure to curtail Israeli transgressions. He highlighted a key reason for this lack of empathy: the US administration barely had any interaction with Palestinians. Although there was robust engagement with Israelis, Ahmed reports there were only five State Department officials in direct contact with Palestinians.
Of all the avoidable tragedies Ahmed’s work highlights, the fact that you need to talk to people on the other side of a conflict to remember that they are human, truly resonates. That recognition of humanity is then enshrined in policy and decision-making.
This need for engagement is too often simplified and understood as the need for backchannels during a crisis. No doubt, informal, person-to-person contact is invaluable when de-escalation is required. Recall the secret meetings that avoided nuclear war during the Cuban Missile Crisis or — closer to home — the DGMO hotline that prevented the May 2025 Pakistan-India conflict from escalating further.
But backchannels cannot substitute for broader diplomatic and societal engagement, the type that goes past mere coordination to empathic connection; the type the Americans have in place with Israel, but did not bother to develop with Palestine, even at the height of humanitarian crisis during the darkest days of the Gaza war. It is a point that should be emphasised in the context of mainstream diplomacy at a time when most Western governments are reducing global diplomatic staff and closing embassies, usually as a cost-cutting measure, leaving them with few personal touch points in regions in perma-crisis.
But these lessons also apply domestically. The political polarisation of Western countries is increasingly attributed to a breakdown of engagement between urban and rural residents, the rich and the poor, and between different racial and ethnic communities. This, in turn, is blamed on everything from the isolation wrought by social media to the claw-back of government funding for community spaces.
We are not absolved from complicity closer to home. It is difficult to imagine Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz making the divisive comments she did about threats to Punjab primarily emanating from regional provinces without years of political suppression and polarised rhetoric between provinces, particularly with Balochistan and KP.
Without more access and engagement, compatriots cannot empathise with each other’s challenges. That engagement should be encouraged across all levels of provincial governments, but equally across society, whether in the form of more scholarships, economic ties, tourism, arts engagement or the lifting of media censorship. Without engaging, we’re in danger of forgetting each other’s humanity, and so exacerbating rather than allaying tensions. 
The writer is a political and integrity risk analyst.

title: Extraction and delivery
author: none@none.com (Umair Javed)
content:
AS the debate on changing provincial boundaries and decentralisation rages on, it is worth taking a step back to see what is at stake here. What are the main problems that require attention and which have made several people, including entrenched insiders, declare that the current system is ‘broken’?
The biggest issue being sidestepped by everyone involved (except opposition parties) remains constitutional rule and legitimacy of the state. The current discourse chooses to ignore this, considering it either taboo or a foregone conclusion. Bringing it up seems particularly futile in this discussion given how little it bears on those making decisions and increasingly with those tasked with interrogating these decisions.
    
The second issue is macroeconomic growth, or the absence thereof. What changes are needed to the form of the state that can help kickstart broad-based and sustained capital accumulation? What needs to be done to make the state fiscally more viable?
The third issue is social development, and the slowdown in improvement of basic education, health, and other human capability-related indicators. What strategy or approach will help break through the current plateau, marked by a slowdown in literacy rate improvement, a persistently large number of out-of-school children, poor learning outcomes, and no considerable progress on health indicators?
When the interior minister talks about a system collapse, the primary subject of this collapse is the state. The Pakistani state, like every other modern state, is engaged in a variety of tasks, none of which it seems to be doing too well. Broadly these tasks can be clubbed under two domains — extraction (getting something from its population) and delivery (doing something for or to the population). There is a third domain — regulation (setting boundaries or implementing rules for various things that private actors may be doing) — as well but we’ll keep that to one side for now.
There is no one-size-fits-all approach for the many developmental challenges confronting Pakistan today.
The historical record on extraction and delivery is generally poor. Extracting taxes from anyone other than a captive population has proven to be a challenge. Regulating private behaviour, from polluting emissions to urban sprawl to inter-gender interactions, has been difficult as well. And delivering basic services — law and order, education, health — remains highly uneven across rural-urban and provincial lines.
If one thinks about the state as the core of a governing system, the track record so far provides ample grounds for a complete overhaul. But a key question to ask is: do all of these functions require an overhaul of the same type?
It is possible to look at the exceedingly few examples of success on part of the state in each domain as a blueprint of sorts for what works, especially when thinking about administrative changes.
What type of extraction has the state done well and where has it failed? In recent years, the state has done a ‘good’ job of getting people to pay for expensive electricity at cost, rather than delay tariff revisions or provide blanket subsidies. This is an example of a reform that is not really productivity enhancing, but it is certainly something that the state was not doing a decade and a half ago.
    
Similarly, the state has been successful at extracting more taxes from the formal sector and the salaried segment of the population in recent years. This is both by raising the tax rate and by making it ever difficult for the formal sector to avoid its share through an entrenched withholding tax regime. This has happened even while the state has failed to bring many sections of the population into the tax net.
When we review the evidence on what enables some types of extraction over others, the absence of discretion and fragmentation of functions comes out as a possible factor. In the case of electricity bills and withholding taxes, the state has centralised collection and removed discretion from its own functions. Local state functionaries have some leeway, sure, but by and large people have no option but to comply and pay directly to the state. In contrast, where economic activity has to be documented by state functionaries themselves (ie, a situation of increased discretion) local politics and influence come into play.
On the other hand, the evidence on delivery points in the opposite direction. The biggest gains in social development took place during times of greater decentralisation. When schools were being managed at the school council/local level, improvements in literacy rates and enrolment happened at a faster rate. Similarly, greater autonomy for basic health units and hospitals (with requisite oversight) allowed them to respond to actual patient-level challenges more effectively.
Even in delivering basic municipal infrastructure — sanitation and sewage, roadworks — decentralised decision-making and expenditure (between 2002-2008) proved to be more effective.
Since province-level centralisation took hold in 2011, gains in key delivery areas of health and education have slowed down. In some parts of the country, outcomes have stagnated altogether. The challenge of delivering to hard-to-access populations has become far more acute.
Given this admittedly speculative review of patterns in both extraction and delivery, it is clear there is no one-size-fits-all approach for the many developmental challenges confronting Pakistan today. In domains of extraction, there is an urgent need to reduce discretion and fragmentation of state authority, perhaps even with the use of automated structures in whatever form.
In delivery related domains, we likely need even more discretion and fragmentation of the state, via substantive decentralisation that devolves decision-making and accountability down to the level where delivery is supposed to take place.
The writer teaches politics and sociology at Lums.

The state's fundamental tasks can be broadly categorized into extraction (obtaining resources from the population) and delivery (providing services to the population), alongside regulation.
Successful state extraction functions (e.g., tax collection, utility payments) have historically been achieved by reducing discretion and centralizing collection mechanisms.

Effective state delivery functions (e.g., education, health, municipal services) have demonstrated better outcomes through greater decentralization and local-level autonomy, allowing for more responsive governance.
facts: The state successfully extracted payments for expensive electricity at cost, a reform that was not being implemented a decade and a half ago.
Gains in key delivery areas of health and education have slowed down significantly since province-level centralization took hold in 2011.
Decentralized decision-making and expenditure between 2002-2008 proved more effective in delivering basic municipal infrastructure like sanitation and roadworks.
academicReferences: The 18th Amendment to the Constitution of Pakistan (A landmark constitutional reform for provincial autonomy and decentralization)
National Finance Commission (NFC) Award (Mechanism for the distribution of financial resources between the federal and provincial governments in Pakistan)
Pakistan Economic Survey (An annual publication providing data and analysis on Pakistan's economic performance and social indicators)

title: Political disconnect
author: none@none.com (Maleeha Lodhi)
content:
THE disconnect between the government and public concerns could not be starker. While people worry about their economic situation the government is focused on altering the country’s provincial structure. According to the latest Ipsos poll, three in four people believe the country is headed in the wrong direction. The economy and especially inflation are their top concerns. A majority of respondents also said they do not view the economy as strong.
It is this low public confidence and pessimism about the future that should concern the government rather than seeking to redraw the provincial map for ill-defined objectives. So far it hasn’t offered any coherent rationale for carving out more provinces. It has also not conducted any study on an issue of such consequence.
    
Although speculation had long been rife about the hybrid government’s intentions it was Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi who made a public pitch for new provinces in July. Planning Minister Ahsan Iqbal went further, calling for 15 additional provinces. Each province, he said, should be subdivided into three. As an alternative, he proposed 160 district governments. He argued that establishing more administrative units would deliver effective governance and better social outcomes.
The proposal provoked a furious response from the ruling party’s ally, PPP, which opposed any plan to divide Sindh. The party got the Sindh Assembly to adopt a resolution rejecting the division of the province or creation of new administrative units. The MQM, which has long wanted Karachi as a separate province, boycotted the session. It said its proposals were not incorporated in the resolution, including establishing new administrative units. The resolution declared “Sindh is one and shall remain one” and “unequivocally rejected any proposal, plan, scheme or constitutional arrangement … which sought to divide Sindh … or create any new province out of its territory”.
Technical fixes are no panacea that will miraculously solve the country’s problems.
The government’s attempt to start a debate seemed to flounder and spin out of control after its key coalition partner came out in strong opposition. A senior PPP leader questioned Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif’s silence and asked him to state his position publicly. Another PPP leader accused federal ministers pushing for new provinces of having a “fake mandate”. Meanwhile, PML-N ministers themselves issued contradictory statements. Rather than clarifying matters, this compounded the confusion and exposed divisions within the party. Punjab Chief Minister Maryam Nawaz is also said to be opposed to any division of her province.
    
The joint parliamentary opposition comprising PTI, JUI-F and other smaller parties rejected any plan to divide provinces at its inaugural meeting in late August. Earlier, JUI-F chief Maulana Fazlur Rahman argued this was not the time to divide provinces given the country’s troubled economic and security situation. PTI is now planning a multiparty conference of the opposition on the issue. The party itself has yet to enunciate a clear public position. In the past, it advocated creating a new province in south Punjab. Some PTI leaders say the party opposes changes under “an illegitimate and fraudulent set-up”. The party chairman, however, has urged consultations and said any hasty decision would “harm the federation”. Meanwhile, the leader of the National Party in Balochistan has said creating new provinces would only exacerbate present tensions.
None of this has deterred federal ministers from continuing to insist on administrative restructuring. Mohsin Naqvi declared this was essential and no one can stop it. But he added it will only happen with the “will of the people”. He wasn’t walking back from his proposal. His statement implied a referendum might be held to ascertain the ‘will of the people’. Such a move would be deeply controversial and divisive. It would also lack credibility given the history of dubious referendums conducted by past military governments. Questions have also been raised about whether a referendum can constitutionally be used to create new provinces.
Proponents of ‘reform’ in the hybrid government ignore the fact that their proposal has already divided the country. It is clear that there is no political consensus on the issue. Consensus cannot be manufactured or coerced. While the government has rammed controversial constitutional amendments and other laws through parliament, using the same method to reorder the provincial structure carries much greater risks. Given the far-reaching consequences of the change and the opposition it faces across the country, the implications would be serious. If pursued, it would further undermine national cohesion and deepen polarisation.
    
There is a clear constitutional procedure to change provincial boundaries. A referendum cannot override that. Any change requires two steps. First a resolution passed by a two-thirds majority in the relevant provincial assembly. Second a constitutional amendment adopted by a two-thirds majority in both the National Assembly and Senate. This effectively gives affected provinces a veto over any change. This requirement cannot be bypassed. Any political manoeuvre to circumvent this will be a disaster.
There is no doubt that the governance system needs to be improved. Government should be brought closer to the people to ensure their voices are heard and for better service delivery. But this goal can be realised by empowering local government. It is the third tier of government that needs to be strengthened through functional local bodies as mandated by the Constitution.
Improving governance requires more than a technical fix. Above all, it demands an environment grounded in the rule of law. It needs accountability of both leaders and institutions. Administrative changes cannot substitute for competent leadership — with a clear vision and sense of purpose — who are legitimately elected. Good governance also requires prudent policies and much-needed economic reforms shaped and overseen by capable professionals.
This is not an argument against administrative change. It is an effort to emphasise three points. First, drawing new provincial lines is not a panacea that will miraculously solve the country’s problems. As noted above, other aspects of governance matter far more. Map-drawing and not fixing fundamentals is meaningless. Second, such changes do not figure among the public’s governance concerns, which are very different. Ignoring those priorities and focusing just on technical fixes will only show how out of touch the government is with people. Third, without broad national consensus, imposing administrative changes will make a mockery of democracy and serve to divide the country.
The writer is a former ambassador to the US, UK and UN.
Published in Dawn, September 14th, 2026

summary: The government's focus on altering provincial structure disconnects sharply from public concerns, primarily economic hardship and inflation.
There is a significant lack of political consensus, coherent rationale, and proper study for creating new provinces, leading to widespread opposition from various political parties.

The article argues that creating new provinces without broad national consensus and adherence to constitutional procedures (two-thirds majorities in provincial and federal assemblies) risks undermining national cohesion and deepening polarization.

Effective governance should be achieved by empowering local governments, ensuring the rule of law, promoting accountability, and implementing prudent economic reforms, rather than through technical fixes like redrawing provincial maps.
